# Review report — Weekly audit 2026-11-09

> **PARTIAL RUN.** 29 of 52 entries attempted. This is not a baseline audit; everything else is *not checked*.

## Summary

- Coverage: 94 items checked, 88 against outside sources (54 no change, 6 changed, 22 unresolved — mostly comparative wording — 6 inaccessible) and 6 internally. This week's rolling set was the 88 items last verified on 10 Oct whose wording has been edited since, so their current text had never itself been checked. 255 sources behind earlier checks were re-fetched (222 by plain download, 33 in headless Chromium; 234 retrieved): every recorded quotation still matches except ai.gov's old 404 text (already explained on 6 Nov), so no item needed re-verification for a changed source. 185 items have not been re-verified since 10 Oct; they come next.
- 6 new proposals (P-0189 to P-0194) and one revision (P-0161 v2). Google DeepMind said in October it cannot rule out that Gemini 4 Argon reached its biological and cyber uplift CCLs, and built safety cases (P-0189); a METR team has employee-like access at Anthropic and publishes its assessments (P-0190); the Digital Omnibus gives the AI Office supervision of AI systems built on a provider's own GPAI model (P-0191); UK AISI's renamed focus never included 'autonomy' (P-0192); the UK now has a statutory duty for an ICO code on AI and automated decision-making (P-0193, SI 2026/425); Colorado DOI's bias testing depends on rules not yet adopted (P-0194). P-0161 v2 adds Bosnia and Herzegovina's ratification of the CoE AI Convention (28 Oct 2026).
- Awaiting your decision in total: 45 proposals (30 corrections, 1 new entry, 14 questions with drafted options and a recommendation), including the 39 from 6 Nov. P-0187 (White House Accord on Super Intelligence) is still held: Anthropic's 15 Oct post confirms it and Anthropic's signature, but no official full text was found.
- Discovery since 6 Nov: no new framework versions (RSP v3.4, FSF v3.1, Meta v2.1, xAI 30 Jun 2026 edition); no new BIS rule on advanced computing or model weights (Federal Register API); California SB 813 / AB 1405 (chaptered 9 Sep 2026) screened out — they regulate auditors and a designation process from 2028–29, with no developer duties. Leads: OpenAI's reported Preparedness Framework rewrite and paused RL run (Aug 2026) and misalignment-incident disclosure framework (Sep 2026) — openai.com refuses automated clients, so unverified.
- Nothing was applied (no answers on the page since 6 Nov), so the map's content date stays 11 Oct 2026. Still unreachable: coe.int, openai.com, ico.org.uk, ftc.gov, meti.go.jp; California's statute text was read from the Legislative Counsel's public bulk download instead of the blocked website. Tooling: source fetch now requests compressed content, fixing unreadable gzip pages.

### P-0151 v1 — xAI entry: SpaceX acquired xAI and the site now names SpaceX Super Intelligence LLC (SpaceXSI) — rename or note?

`question` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: medium · change-hash `26eb2735ce2e`

**Question for you:** SpaceX acquired xAI on 2 Feb 2026. x.ai now titles its safety page 'Safety at SpaceXSI', its footer reads '© 2026 SpaceX Super Intelligence LLC', and the consumer terms (27 Oct 2026) are an agreement with SpaceX Super Intelligence LLC. The framework itself (effective 30 Jun 2026, re-hosted at a new URL after the old one went 404) is unchanged and still titled and issued by 'xAI LLC'; the Grok 4.7 card (Sep 2026) called SpaceXAI a DBA of XAI LLC. Options: (a) keep the entry name, which matches the document's own title, and record the ownership and rebrand in desc (recommended); (b) rename the entry to 'SpaceXSI (xAI) Frontier AI Framework' and add the same desc note; (c) keep as is.

**Why it matters:** Readers following the map's link land on a SpaceXSI-branded page; the map does not say who now owns or publishes the framework.

**Reasoning:** Recommend (a): the map names L6 entries after the framework document, and the document is still 'xAI Frontier Artificial Intelligence Framework' issued by 'xAI LLC' (xai-fw#w2, #w11); the ownership change (xai-joins#j1, spacex-upd#u1) and the new operator name (xai-safety#x1, #x3; xai-tos#t2) are hard facts for desc. The relationship between XAI LLC and SpaceX Super Intelligence LLC (rename vs. new entity) is not stated in any source found, so the desc avoids asserting it.

### P-0157 v1 — NAAIMES elicitation note: the Jul 2026 guidance covers automated evaluations only, not jailbreaks or agentic scaffolding

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: high · change-hash `1ae6206953b9`

**Change**

- **`aisi-net` · coverage · elicit**

  Current:

  > Pools elicitation techniques (prompting strategies, agentic scaffolding, jailbreaks) so that what one institute discovers is available to others. Most useful for catching sandbagging or capability gaps that single-institute testing might miss.

  Proposed:

  > The first best-practice guidance (Jul 2026) advises third-party evaluators on capability elicitation in automated evaluations: iterating on prompts and inference settings, with tuning data kept separate from reported results. Red-team testing and agentic evaluations are out of its scope.

**Why it matters:** The note says the network pools jailbreak and agentic-scaffolding techniques and helps catch sandbagging. Its only published guidance explicitly excludes red-team testing and agentic evaluations, and no network document mentions sandbagging.

**Reasoning:** The guidance's scope section limits it to automated evaluations and lists red-team testing and agentic evaluations as out of scope; section C.1.2 sets out elicitation practices (prompt iteration, inference settings, disjoint tuning and evaluation sets) for third-party evaluators.

### P-0158 v1 — NAAIMES timing coverage: no source shows the network coordinating pre-deployment access

`question` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: medium · change-hash `6de63921a340`

**Question for you:** No network document shows NAAIMES coordinating pre-deployment evaluation access between members and labs. Keep the timing coverage note, or remove it?

**Why it matters:** The note presents an undocumented function as fact. Pre-deployment access is arranged bilaterally by individual institutes (e.g. UK AISI, CAISI), not by the network.

**Reasoning:** The network's published work from Dec 2025 to Jul 2026 concerns measurement science and best practice for third-party evaluators. The UK, NIST and AISI pages describe knowledge exchange and best practice, and the Jul 2026 guidance contains nothing on deployment timing or access. Removing the note follows RUBRIC §6: coverage notes are claims and must be supported.

**Evidence**

### P-0159 v1 — UNESCO Recommendation: monitoring is by Member State reporting to the Executive Board, not the Readiness Assessment Methodology

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: high · change-hash `208035846361`

**Change**

- **`unesco` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Transparency and human oversight are core principles, but the recommendation imposes no reporting or audit obligations. Implementation is monitored by UNESCO's Readiness Assessment Methodology.

  Proposed:

  > Transparency and human oversight are core principles, but the recommendation imposes no reporting or audit obligations on AI developers. Member States report on implementation in periodic consultations examined by UNESCO's Executive Board and General Conference (first consolidated report 2025, next 2029); the Readiness Assessment Methodology is a voluntary diagnostic for interested countries.

**Why it matters:** The note says implementation is monitored by the Readiness Assessment Methodology. That is a voluntary self-assessment tool for countries; the formal monitoring is by the Executive Board, using consolidated reports on Member States' implementation.

UNESCO's Legal Affairs page lists it as a Recommendation "for which monitoring the Executive Board is responsible". ### P-0162 v1 — EU AI Office: evaluation powers are Art. 92 evaluations and access requests, not pre-deployment access

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: medium · change-hash `a40a3807cc58`

**Change**

- **`eu-aio` · coverage · eval**

  Current:

  > Can request evaluations from GPAI providers, including pre-deployment access for systemic-risk models. The Scientific Panel of independent experts advises on what to request and how to interpret results.

  Proposed:

  > Can evaluate GPAI models itself or through appointed independent experts, requesting access via APIs or source code (Art. 92); the Act gives it no pre-release access, but Code signatories commit to a Safety and Security Model Report, available to the Office by the time a model is placed on the market. The Scientific Panel of independent experts advises on what to request and how to interpret results.

**Why it matters:** The note tells readers the Office has pre-deployment access to systemic-risk models; the AI Act gives it no such power, which matters for comparing it with AISIs that do test before release.

**Reasoning:** Art. 92 lets the AI Office conduct evaluations itself or via appointed independent experts and request access through APIs or source code (ai-act p1–p3); nothing in Arts 88–94 gives access before a model is placed on the market (ai-act p8). The Office conducts evaluations rather than 'requesting evaluations from providers'; it can request providers' Art. 53/55 documentation (p7). The closest pre-release element is the GPAI Code: signatories create a Model Report before placing a model on the market and give the Office access by that time (cop-ss p1–p2), with up to 15 business days' delay allowed (p3).

**Evidence**

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: high · change-hash `5d22a2cb490d`

**Change**

  Current:

  > Established the dominant external methodology for scheming detection — controlled stress-tests for whether models strategically deceive evaluators, exfiltrate, or sandbag. The conceptual frame (deceptive alignment, mesa-optimisation) predates Apollo, but their 2024 paper was the inflection point that brought scheming evaluations into mainstream lab practice — cited as input to GDM's FSF v2, used in OpenAI's o1 system card and Preparedness v2, and referenced in Anthropic's Claude system cards.

### P-0168 v1 — CAIS: MMLU is not a CAIS benchmark, and Humanity's Last Exam is a capability benchmark

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: high · change-hash `6b7e73777625`

**Change**

- **`cais` · context**

  Current:

  > Field-building NGO running widely-used safety benchmarks (MMLU, Humanity's Last Exam, WMDP weapons-of-mass-destruction proxy), research grants, and policy advocacy. The May 2023 'Statement on AI Risk' — a one-sentence declaration that mitigating extinction risk from AI should be a global priority — was signed by leading lab CEOs (Altman, Hassabis, Amodei) and shaped the 2023-2024 AI-risk discourse. In June 2026 expanded leadership with former xAI engineer Devin Kim as President and established the Frontier Security Institute as a DC-based national-security affiliate.

  Proposed:

  > Field-building NGO running widely-used benchmarks (Humanity's Last Exam, WMDP weapons-of-mass-destruction proxy), research grants, and policy advocacy. The May 2023 'Statement on AI Risk' — a one-sentence declaration that mitigating extinction risk from AI should be a global priority — was signed by leading lab CEOs (Altman, Hassabis, Amodei) and shaped the 2023-2024 AI-risk discourse. In June 2026 expanded leadership with former xAI engineer Devin Kim as President and established the Frontier Security Institute as a DC-based national-security affiliate.

- **`cais` · coverage · eval**

  Current:

  > Hosts and publishes safety benchmarks (MMLU, Humanity's Last Exam, WMDP) that feed into lab framework evaluations and AISI testing.

  Proposed:

  > Hosts and publishes benchmarks (Humanity's Last Exam, WMDP, Virology Capabilities Test) that feed into lab framework evaluations and AISI testing.

**Why it matters:** MMLU predates CAIS and is a general knowledge test, so listing it as a CAIS safety benchmark misattributes it; HLE is labelled a capability benchmark by CAIS itself.

**Reasoning:** MMLU is a 2020/21 paper by Hendrycks et al. at universities, a test of 'multitask accuracy' requiring 'extensive world knowledge' (mmlu p1–p3); CAIS's research page does not list it (cais-research p4) and classes Humanity's Last Exam as a 'Capability Benchmark' (p1), while listing WMDP and the Virology Capabilities Test (p2–p3). The lab-evaluation link is evidenced: Anthropic used VCT in Claude Opus 5.5's biological-risk evaluations (opus55 p2) and OpenAI ran WMDP splits for o1 (o1-card p2).

### P-0172 v1 — New L4 entry? AEF-1, the AI Evaluator Forum's standard now cited by the EU AI Office

`question` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: medium · change-hash `f1e2216b24e7`

**Question for you:** How should the map record AEF-1, which the EU AI Office now cites as the minimum for external-evaluator contracts under the GPAI Code?

**Why it matters:** A voluntary evaluator standard became part of how the EU AI Office judges Code compliance for external evaluations, a new link between Layer 4 evaluators and the EU regime.

**Reasoning:** AEF-1 (v1, 4 Dec 2025) sets operating conditions and a checklist for independent evaluations (aef1 p1–p2, p5). The AI Office's 21 Oct 2026 workshop report says independence of external evaluators under Code Measures 3.2/3.5 should be ensured by contractual safeguards including at least AEF-1's Analytic Autonomy and Transparent Methods sections (ec-evalreq-report p1–p2; ec-evalreq p1). AVERI coauthored it (averi-about p1); METR's Frontier Risk Report used its checklist (aef1 p3). It meets RUBRIC §1 (identifiable text, material via Code compliance, attributable to the Forum, applied by the AI Office); SCOPE B3 admits a standard 'used for regulatory compliance'. Option a recommended because the mechanism is distinct from its authors; b is a lighter alternative.

### P-0174 v1 — Australia eSafety: the Online Safety Act 2021 confers no AI-specific authority; AI duties come through codes and standards made under it

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: high · change-hash `5a60103584f9`

**Change**

- **`au-esafety` · desc**

  Current:

  > World's first online safety regulator (established 2015), with AI-specific enforcement authority under the Online Safety Act 2021.

  Proposed:

  > World's first online safety regulator (established 2015). The Online Safety Act 2021 contains no AI-specific provisions; AI obligations come through industry codes and standards made under it (e.g. the 2024 standard covering high-impact generative AI services).

**Why it matters:** The entry tells readers that Australian law gives eSafety AI-specific powers. It does not: eSafety applies general online-safety powers, and AI enters only through instruments it makes under the Act.

**Reasoning:** The current compilation of the Act (No. 4, 12 Sep 2026) contains no reference to artificial intelligence, generative systems, algorithms or chatbots. Section 145 lets the Commissioner determine industry standards; the 2024 DIS standard, made under s 145, defines a 'high impact generative AI DIS'. So the AI-specific element is the standard, not the Act.

**Evidence**

- **S-0338** Online Safety Act 2021 (Compilation No. 4, 12 September 2026) — <https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2021A00076/2026-09-12/2026-09-12/text/original/epub/OEBPS/document_1/document_1.html>

The Act confers general online-safety powers (complaints, removal notices, codes, standards, penalties) with no AI-specific provision.
  _Supports:_ No AI-specific provision in the Act

### P-0178 v1 — New entry: Japan AI Basic Plan (Cabinet decision; second plan of 14 Jul 2026 commits to frontier-AI evaluation by J-AISI)

`addition` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: medium · change-hash `54190aaf5354`

**Change**

- **New entry `jp-aiplan`** — Japan AI Basic Plan · Layer 2 · jur `as` · pow 2 · active · https://www8.cao.go.jp/cstp/ai/ai_plan/ai_plan.html

> Cabinet-decided national AI plan under Art. 18 of the AI Promotion Act. First plan Dec 23, 2025; second plan Jul 14, 2026, to be revised in principle annually.

> The government's roadmap under the AI Promotion Act, assigning measures to ministries. The second plan responds to agentic AI and AI-enabled cyberattacks: it commits to strengthening J-AISI, including proactive evaluation of highly capable frontier AI for national-security risks, and to leading international discussion of frontier-AI governance. Like the US AI Action Plan, a policy document with no binding obligations on developers; it encourages voluntary steps.

  - _eval_: Commits to building J-AISI's technical evaluation capacity, including proactive evaluation of highly capable frontier AI from a national-security perspective, and to linking results to ministries' systems and guidelines.
  - _update_: Reviewed and revised as needed, in principle annually; the second plan (Jul 2026) followed the first (Dec 2025) within seven months.

- **new connection `jp-aiplan` ↔ `jp-ai`**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > The Basic Plan is decided under Art. 18 of the AI Promotion Act

- **new connection `jp-aiplan` ↔ `other-aisis`**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > Second plan commits to strengthening J-AISI's frontier-AI evaluation

**Why it matters:** The map has Japan's AI Promotion Act but not the Cabinet plan that implements it. The July 2026 plan is Japan's first government commitment to evaluate highly capable frontier AI for national-security risks, which bears directly on frontier-AI governance.

**Reasoning:** The Cabinet Office page shows the second plan decided by the Cabinet on 14 Jul 2026 and the first on 23 Dec 2025. The plan's text states its Art. 18 basis, the AISI commitments, the voluntary approach and annual revision. It meets RUBRIC §1 (identifiable Cabinet decision, attributable to the Cabinet/AI Strategic Headquarters, material through the frontier-AI evaluation commitments). Layer 2 and pow 2 follow the US AI Action Plan precedent (policy document of recommended actions, pow 2).

### P-0179 v1 — Singapore IMDA: enforceability pow 3 or pow 2?

`question` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: medium · change-hash `b16996654c4f`

**Question for you:** IMDA is rated pow 3 (hard law, weak enforcement), but every AI instrument the entry describes (Model AI Governance Framework, AI Verify, chatbot transparency guidelines, testing starter kits) is voluntary guidance. Should IMDA be pow 2 (soft/advisory)?

**Why it matters:** pow 3 implies a binding instrument with weak enforcement. The entry presents no binding AI instrument from IMDA, so the rating overstates its legal force on AI developers.

**Reasoning:** RUBRIC §4 puts government-issued non-binding guidance and voluntary codes at pow 2. IMDA's own AI page describes its frameworks as guidance and its newest instruments as voluntary guidelines; the entry's context itself says Singapore 'emphasises voluntary frameworks'. Option b matches the rubric and the entry text. No prose count needs changing (stats count only pow 1 and pow 4, and are derived).

**Evidence**

- **S-0260** Artificial Intelligence in Singapore | IMDA — <https://www.imda.gov.sg/about-imda/emerging-technologies-and-research/artificial-intelligence>
  primary · retrieved 2026-11-09 · access: ok via browser
  Using AI Responsibly — Transparency Guidelines for Generative AI Chatbots:
  > These voluntary guidelines take a first step towards closing this gap, beginning with generative AI chatbots, the application with the widest consumer reach and the subject of considerable public concern.
  _Supports:_ Chatbot transparency guidelines are voluntary
- **S-0260** Artificial Intelligence in Singapore | IMDA — <https://www.imda.gov.sg/about-imda/emerging-technologies-and-research/artificial-intelligence>
  primary · retrieved 2026-11-09 · access: ok via browser
  Using AI Responsibly — Starter Kit for Testing LLM-based Applications:
  > consolidating emerging best practices from industry and government into practical, voluntary guidelines
  _Supports:_ Testing starter kit is voluntary guidance
- **S-0260** Artificial Intelligence in Singapore | IMDA — <https://www.imda.gov.sg/about-imda/emerging-technologies-and-research/artificial-intelligence>
  primary · retrieved 2026-11-09 · access: ok via browser
  Using AI Responsibly — Model AI Governance Framework:
  > The framework provides detailed and readily implementable guidance to private sector organisations to address key ethical and governance issues when deploying AI solutions.
  _Supports:_ Model Framework is guidance

**Uncertainty:** IMDA is also a statutory regulator with penalty powers in other areas (e.g. online-safety codes under the Broadcasting Act), which were not checked. If those powers are counted as they are for Ofcom and eSafety, pow 4 would be the consistent rating; that would need a source check and a desc that names the power. imda's entry metadata is in another group's item list, which may raise the same question.

**May need reconsideration if accepted**

### P-0180 v1 — Illinois AI Safety Measures Act: the Agency can also levy disclosure penalties, and incident reporting binds all frontier developers

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: high · change-hash `342b39e22b0d`

**Change**

- **`il-aisma` · context**

  Current:

  > Third state frontier-AI statute, built on the SB 53 / RAISE template: large frontier developers publish a frontier AI framework, file disclosure statements, and report critical safety incidents to the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and the AG within 72 hours; all frontier developers publish transparency reports at deployment. Unlike SB 53 and RAISE, it requires large frontier developers to retain an independent third-party auditor every year. AG enforcement only.

  Proposed:

  > Third state frontier-AI statute, built on the SB 53 / RAISE template: large frontier developers publish a frontier AI framework and file disclosure statements; all frontier developers report critical safety incidents to the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and the AG within 72 hours and publish transparency reports at deployment. Unlike SB 53 and RAISE, it requires large frontier developers to retain an independent third-party auditor every year. Penalties for framework, audit and reporting failures are recovered only by the AG; the Agency can itself levy $1,000-a-day penalties for a missing or false disclosure statement.

- **`il-aisma` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Annual independent third-party audit of framework compliance from 2028, with a published summary; disclosure statements filed with the Agency from 2027; AG-only civil penalties up to $1M first / $3M subsequent.

  Proposed:

  > Annual independent third-party audit of framework compliance from 2028, with a published summary; disclosure statements filed with the Agency from 2027; AG-only civil penalties up to $1M first / $3M subsequent, plus Agency penalties of $1,000 a day for a missing or false disclosure statement.

**Why it matters:** 'AG enforcement only' is wrong: the Act gives the Illinois Emergency Management Agency its own penalty power over disclosure statements. The context also assigns incident reporting to large frontier developers only, but the duty applies to every frontier developer.

**Reasoning:** Sec. 25(b) reserves the $1M / $3M civil penalties to actions brought exclusively by the AG, but Sec. 18(e) separately lets the Agency, after notice and hearing, levy $1,000 per day for failing to file or correct a disclosure statement. Sec. 15(c) puts the 72-hour incident duty on 'a frontier developer', not only large ones.

### P-0181 v1 — Colorado: SB 24-205 was not repealed before its Jun 30, 2026 date; the repeal takes effect Jan 1, 2027 and a court order bars enforcement

  Proposed:

  > Effective Jan 1, 2027. SB 26-189 was signed before SB 24-205's delayed Jun 30, 2026 start, but its repeal-and-reenactment takes effect only on Jan 1, 2027; an Apr 27, 2026 federal court order bars enforcement of SB 24-205 pending AG rulemaking and a ruling in xAI v. Weiser. No lifecycle-review obligation.

**Why it matters:** Readers are told SB 24-205 never reached its enforcement date. On the statutes, its delayed Jun 30, 2026 date passed before the repeal took effect; what stops enforcement is the court order.

Weiser.

  > AI Basic Act. In force Jan 22, 2026. One-year grace period — penalties (capped ~$21k per violation) begin Jan 22, 2027.

  Proposed:

  > AI Basic Act. In force Jan 22, 2026. MSIT is deferring fines (capped ~$21k per violation) for at least one year, a policy grace period not set in the Act.

### P-0183 v1 — Japan AI Promotion Act: the AI Strategic Headquarters sits in the Cabinet, with its secretariat in the Cabinet Office

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: high · change-hash `88b4ee139cba`

**Change**

- **`index.html`**

  Current:

  > Establishes the AI Strategic Headquarters under the Cabinet Office to coordinate sectoral guidance.

  Proposed:

  > Establishes the AI Strategic Headquarters in the Cabinet (headed by the Prime Minister; secretariat in the Cabinet Office) to coordinate sectoral guidance.

**Why it matters:** Placing the HQ 'under the Cabinet Office' understates it: the statute places it in the Cabinet itself, headed by the Prime Minister.

**Reasoning:** Art. 19 places the HQ 'in the Cabinet' (内閣に); Art. 22 makes the Prime Minister its head; Art. 26 assigns only its administrative affairs to the Cabinet Office (内閣府).

### P-0191 v1 — EU AI Act · Accountability: since the Digital Omnibus the AI Office, not national authorities, supervises AI systems built on a provider's own GPAI model

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: high · change-hash `7827235c8c95`

**Change**

- **`eu-aia` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Mandatory incident reporting to the EU AI Office for systemic-risk GPAI; market-surveillance authorities handle high-risk systems. The Office can request models, order recalls, and fine GPAI providers up to €15M / 3% global revenue.

  Proposed:

  > Mandatory incident reporting to the EU AI Office for systemic-risk GPAI; market-surveillance authorities handle high-risk systems, except that under the 2026 Digital Omnibus the AI Office supervises AI systems built on a provider's own GPAI model and receives their serious-incident reports. The Office can request models, order recalls, and fine GPAI providers up to €15M / 3% global revenue.

**Why it matters:** A frontier lab's own AI products built on its own GPAI model now answer to the AI Office, including serious-incident reports for high-risk ones; the note says only national market-surveillance authorities handle high-risk systems.

**Reasoning:** Reg. 2026/1744 replaces Art. 75(1): the AI Office is exclusively competent for AI systems based on GPAI models where model and system come from the same provider, and new Art. 75(1a) routes those providers' high-risk serious-incident reports to the AI Office instead of Art. 73's national authorities. The eu-aio entry already describes these powers; this aligns the Act's own accountability note.

**Evidence**

- **S-0041** Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) — <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=OJ:L_202601744>
  primary · retrieved 2026-11-09 · access: ok via browser · adopted 2026-07-08, published 2026-07, in_force 2026-07-27

### P-0192 v1 — UK AISI: the Feb 2025 rename named chemical/biological weapons, cyber attacks and crime as its focus, not autonomy

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: high · change-hash `5b88fa6f0281`

**Change**

- **`uk-aisi` · context**

  Current:

  > Conducts pre-deployment evaluations of frontier models under voluntary access agreements with major labs; publishes red-teaming and jailbreaking research. The Feb 2025 rename to 'AI Security Institute' narrowed focus toward national-security-adjacent risks (cyber, bio, autonomy) and aligned framing with US CAISI. The 2024 King's Speech promised legislation on developers of the most powerful AI models, but no government bill was introduced and the May 2026 King's Speech announced none, so its access remains voluntary — labs could withdraw. The inaugural Frontier AI Trends Report (Dec 2025) draws on two years of evaluating 30+ frontier models.

  Proposed:

  > Conducts pre-deployment evaluations of frontier models under voluntary access agreements with major labs; publishes red-teaming and jailbreaking research. The Feb 2025 rename to 'AI Security Institute' narrowed focus toward national-security-adjacent risks (chemical and biological weapons, cyber attacks, crime such as fraud and child sexual abuse) and aligned framing with US CAISI. The 2024 King's Speech promised legislation on developers of the most powerful AI models, but no government bill was introduced and the May 2026 King's Speech announced none, so its access remains voluntary — labs could withdraw. The inaugural Frontier AI Trends Report (Dec 2025) draws on two years of evaluating 30+ frontier models.

**Why it matters:** The parenthesis tells readers what the rename refocused AISI on. The official announcement names chemical and biological weapons, cyber attacks and crime; it does not mention autonomy, so the map misstates the stated focus.

**Reasoning:** The 14 Feb 2025 GOV.UK release says the new name reflects a focus on risks 'such as how the technology can be used to develop chemical and biological weapons, how it can be used to carry out cyber-attacks, and enable crimes such as fraud and child sexual abuse' (aisi-rename p1); 'autonom' does not occur in it (p2). Autonomy remains one of AISI's research areas on its About page, but that is not what the rename announced. The rest of the paragraph checks out: pre-deployment testing and lab collaboration (aisi-about p1–p2), voluntary collaborations (aisi-devsec p1; aisi-bestpractice p1–p2), jailbreak and red-teaming research (aisi-trends p2–p3), the 2024 King's Speech commitment (ks2024 p1), no AI bill in the 2026 King's Speech or its briefing notes (ks2026 p1; ks2026-notes p1), and the Dec 2025 Trends Report covering 30+ systems over two years (aisi-trends-pdf p1; aisi-trends p1).

**Evidence**

  _Supports:_ rename focus: chem/bio weapons, cyber attacks, crime

### P-0193 v1 — UK ICO: 2026 regulations (in force 12 May 2026) require a statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: high · change-hash `bd45c34f2bf5`

**Change**

- **`uk-ico` · context**

  Current:

  > Regulates how organisations train on, deploy, and explain AI under UK GDPR. Its Guidance on AI and Data Protection (2020, updated 2023), part of its AI auditing framework, sets out how it interprets the law on lawful basis, fairness, transparency, and Data Protection Impact Assessments for AI systems; it is not a statutory code and is under review after the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Has investigated Clearview AI, Snap My AI, and others — operates as the UK's de facto frontier-AI privacy regulator alongside any future AISI statutory mandate.

  Proposed:

  > Regulates how organisations train on, deploy, and explain AI under UK GDPR. Its Guidance on AI and Data Protection (2020, updated 2023), part of its AI auditing framework, sets out how it interprets the law on lawful basis, fairness, transparency, and Data Protection Impact Assessments for AI systems; it is not a statutory code, but regulations in force since 12 May 2026 require the regulator to prepare a statutory code of practice on developing and using AI and on automated decision-making. Has investigated Clearview AI, Snap My AI, and others — operates as the UK's de facto frontier-AI privacy regulator alongside any future AISI statutory mandate.

- **`uk-ico` · coverage · mit**

  Current:

  > Non-statutory guidance on fairness, transparency, lawful basis, and explainability for AI deployments touching personal data; the underlying UK GDPR duties are binding.

  Proposed:

  > Non-statutory guidance on fairness, transparency, lawful basis, and explainability for AI deployments touching personal data; the underlying UK GDPR duties are binding. A statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making is required by regulations in force since 12 May 2026.

**Why it matters:** Readers are told the AI guidance is merely 'under review'. In fact a statutory instrument now obliges the regulator to produce a statutory AI and automated decision-making code, which courts and the regulator must take into account once issued — a material change in how binding its AI expectations will be.

**Reasoning:** SI 2026/425, made under DPA 2018 s.124A (inserted by DUAA 2025 s.92), came into force on 12 May 2026 (si2026-425 p1) and requires 'the Commissioner' to prepare a code of practice on processing personal data in relation to developing and using AI and automated decision-making (p2). Since 30 Sep 2026 the Commissioner's functions sit with the Information Commission (duaa-s118 p2; duaa-s119 p1; si2026-1015 p1), so the edit says 'the regulator'. The edit does not say whether a draft has been published.

**Evidence**

  _Supports:_ duty to prepare AI and ADM code

### P-0194 v1 — Colorado DOI context: Regulation 10-1-1 requires documented testing and monitoring; the bias testing and its assumptions await Division rules

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **pending** · confidence: medium · change-hash `021376b449f3`

**Linked:** P-0175

**Change**

- **`co-doi` · context**

  Current:

  > Predates every comprehensive US state AI law. Requires insurance carriers to implement an algorithm and predictive-model governance framework, conduct bias testing, document model assumptions, and submit attestations — applied to life insurers first (Nov 2023), then extended to private passenger auto and health benefit plan insurers (Oct 2025). Followed by similar adoptions in other states via the NAIC Model Bulletin on AI (Dec 2023). The historical anchor that complicates 'first sectoral AI regulator' claims about later state laws like NY RAISE's DFS office.

  Proposed:

  > Predates every comprehensive US state AI law. Requires insurance carriers to implement an algorithm and predictive-model governance framework, document how models are tested, validated and monitored, and submit attestations — applied to life insurers first (Nov 2023), then extended to private passenger auto and health benefit plan insurers (Oct 2025). The quantitative bias testing it references awaits Division rules. Followed by similar adoptions in other states via the NAIC Model Bulletin on AI (Dec 2023). The historical anchor that complicates 'first sectoral AI regulator' claims about later state laws like NY RAISE's DFS office.

**Why it matters:** The context says insurers must 'conduct bias testing' and 'document model assumptions'. The regulation ties both to quantitative testing 'pursuant to requirements established by the Division', which the Division has not adopted; it does require documented testing, validation and monitoring. This is the same problem P-0175 fixes in the Evaluation note, so the two should stay consistent.

**Reasoning:** Amended Reg. 10-1-1 §5.A.6 requires documented policies for design, testing, deployment and monitoring and processes to ensure models are 'documented, tested, and validated' (co-reg1011 p1); §5.A.11 requires a description of quantitative testing 'pursuant to requirements established by the Division', including 'methodology, assumptions, results' (p2, p4); §6.D reports are signed by an officer attesting to compliance (p5). Bulletin B-10.004 (reissued 22 Oct 2025) states the Division has not adopted the quantitative testing regulation (S-0342#1). Effective dates Nov 2023 and Oct 2025 confirmed (p3).

**Evidence**

- **S-0341** Amended Regulation 10-1-1 (3 CCR 702-10), Governance and Risk Management Framework Requirements for Life Insurers', Private Passenger Automobile Insurers', and Health Benefit Plan Insurers' Use of ECDIS, Algorithms, and Predictive Models — <https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1gWvUT_zEn6npupumvYB4Sq_hvh2OZO8y>

### P-0187 v2 — Add the White House Accord on Super Intelligence (29 Sep 2026) as a Layer 5 voluntary cross-firm commitment?

`question` · evidence: **Source access required** · decision: **pending** · confidence: medium · change-hash `a60139638853`

**Question for you:** Six frontier developers' leaders and the President signed a 'Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities' (external auditor/evaluator, independent board committee). It meets RUBRIC §1 on its text, but the only copy found is the American Presidency Project archive; no whitehouse.gov or company copy was found. Add it, and with which jurisdiction?

**Why it matters:** It is the first cross-firm frontier commitment brokered by this administration and the first in which the main US labs commit to independent external assessment and board-level oversight of safety controls.

**Reasoning:** Recommend (a) once an official copy is obtained: it is a cross-firm commitment (Layer 5, like seoul-commit) with no legal force (pow 1, as for seoul-commit and delhi-commit), and its sponsor is the US federal government, so 'us' fits better than 'co'. Until an official White House, Truth Social or company copy is inspected, the evidence is an archive copy only, so the evidence status is 'needs source access'. Update 2026-11-09: Anthropic's own post (15 Oct 2026) now confirms, from a signatory, that the accord exists, that Anthropic signed it, and that signatories pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. ### P-0002 v2 — FAQ: align 'binding laws' with the map's own classifications (internal consistency only)

`change` · evidence: **Internal consistency only (the map checked against itself)** · decision: **accepted** (v2, 2026-10-10) · confidence: medium · change-hash `e33b70d35be3`

_Revised from v1: wording changed, so it needs a fresh decision._

**Change**

- **`index.html`**

  Current:

  > Eight binding instruments in this map carry penalty regimes: the EU AI Act (up to €35M or 7% of global revenue), China's GenAI Measures, Korea's AI Basic Act (~$21k per violation), California SB 53 (up to $1M per violation), the Colorado AI Act, the NY RAISE Act ($1M/$3M), Texas TRAIGA, and US BIS export controls. Most are phasing in; several face active federal preemption challenges in the United States.

  Proposed:

  > Five AI laws in this map are classed as binding with penalties: the EU AI Act (up to €35M or 7% of global revenue), China's GenAI Measures, Korea's AI Basic Act (~$21k per violation), California SB 53 (up to $1M per violation) and the NY RAISE Act ($1M/$3M). Most are phasing in; several face active federal preemption challenges in the United States. The map's wider count of mechanisms that are binding with penalties also includes US BIS export controls and five regulators: the EU AI Office, UK Ofcom, the UK ICO, Australia's eSafety Commissioner and the Colorado Division of Insurance. The map classes the Colorado AI Act and Texas TRAIGA as hard law with weak enforcement, so they are not counted here.

**Why it matters:** The FAQ says eight binding instruments and names Colorado and Texas, while the map classes both as pow 3 and its stats tile counts 11 pow-4 mechanisms. Search engines and LLMs ingest this FAQ.

**Reasoning:** Narrowed from v1. The edit now only aligns the FAQ's list and count with the map's own enforceability classifications and stats tile. It no longer characterises any statute: v1 called Colorado and Texas 'binding statutes' and described the regulators as 'enforcing binding law', both legal claims I had not verified. The penalty figures, 'Most are phasing in' and the preemption sentence are carried over word for word from the current FAQ.

  _Supports:_ The FAQ list versus the pow values and stats tile

**Carried over unchanged, not re-verified:** Penalty figures (EU €35M/7%, Korea ~$21k, California $1M, New York $1M/$3M); 'Most are phasing in' (consistent with the map's status fields, not externally checked); 'several face active federal preemption challenges'

### P-0009 v3 — New connection NY RAISE ↔ Anthropic RSP: RAISE's framework requirement and Anthropic's separate compliance framework

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v3, 2026-10-10) · confidence: medium · change-hash `8d3b104ef303`

_Revised from v2: wording changed, so it needs a fresh decision._

**Linked:** P-0005, P-0010

**Change**

- **new connection `ny-raise` ↔ `rsp`**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > RAISE requires a published frontier AI framework from Jan 2027; Anthropic says it addresses such requirements with documents including its Frontier Compliance Framework, which is separate from the RSP

**Question for you:** Accept this connection on the RSP entry, or prefer no RAISE↔RSP connection until the map decides how to represent compliance frameworks (for example, noting the FCF in the RSP entry, as P-0010 v3 does)?

**Why it matters:** The map connects SB 53 and the EU Code to the RSP but not RAISE. Anthropic names all three as framework-publication requirements it addresses. The official texts now settle both open points: what RAISE requires and from when, and how the compliance document relates to the RSP.

**Reasoning:** Revised from v2 after reading the primary sources. (1) RAISE, as rewritten by Chapter 96 of 2026 (S8828, signed 27 Mar 2026), requires a large frontier developer to 'write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish' a frontier AI framework. It takes effect 1 Jan 2027 (S-0033#2, #3). This RAISE half is now stated in the map's own voice, because the statute was read. (2) Anthropic says SB 53, RAISE and the EU Codes are 'requirements Anthropic addresses through public documentation including its Frontier Compliance Framework' (S-0007#6). The FCF says it 'is distinct from our Responsible Scaling Policy' (S-0010#1). v2 did not say the FCF is a separate document, so a reader would have taken the RSP to be the RAISE compliance route.

### P-0010 v3 — Anthropic RSP: describe the v3 structure (thresholds, ASLs, safeguards, evaluations, timing) and the separate compliance framework

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v3, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `92f0d8ad0842`

_Revised from v2: wording changed, so it needs a fresh decision._

**Linked:** P-0005, P-0013

**Applied together with:** P-0005, P-0006, P-0007, P-0013

**Change**

- **`rsp` · context**

  Current:

  > Defines AI Safety Levels (ASLs) — currently up to ASL-3 — each tied to specific capability evaluations and mandatory safeguards: weight-security tiers, deployment mitigations, model-autonomy controls. The original published framework that set the template for the field; commitments include not deploying at a given ASL until the corresponding mitigations are in place. Subjected to detailed external scrutiny in EU GPAI Code drafting and California SB 53.

  Proposed:

  > Since v3.0 (Feb 2026) the policy separates Anthropic's own plans from more ambitious industry-wide recommendations, which Anthropic says it cannot commit to follow unilaterally. ASLs now label only the safeguards kept for current models (ASL-3). It adds a Frontier Safety Roadmap of public goals (not hard commitments) and Risk Reports every 3–6 months. The original published framework that set the template for the field. Anthropic's documents for California SB 53 and the EU GPAI Code are a separate Frontier Compliance Framework; the RSP remains its voluntary policy.

- **`rsp` · coverage · thresh**

  Current:

  > AI Safety Levels (ASL-1, 2, 3, currently up to ASL-3) trigger graduated safeguards as capabilities cross specified evaluations. The original published framework that set the threshold-and-tier template; SB 53 codifies the underlying norm.

  Proposed:

  > Four capability thresholds (non-novel and novel chemical/biological weapons, misaligned AI in high-stakes settings, automated R&D), each mapped to Anthropic's planned mitigations and to recommended industry-wide mitigations. The original published framework that set the threshold-and-tier template; SB 53 codifies the underlying norm.

- **`rsp` · coverage · eval**

  Current:

  > Pre-deployment evaluations at each ASL covering CBRN, cyber, autonomous-replication, and AI R&D capabilities. Methodology updated as evaluations mature and external evaluator findings come in.

  Proposed:

  > Risk Reports must present capability and alignment evaluations for each threat model, run internally and by external parties as appropriate. Since v3.0 the policy does not pre-specify which evaluations show that a threshold has been crossed.

- **`rsp` · coverage · timing**

  Current:

  > Evaluations run pre-training, pre-deployment, and during ongoing operation; thresholds re-checked as capabilities scale. Among the most comprehensive timing regimes in any framework.

  Proposed:

  > Risk Reports every 3–6 months cover all publicly deployed models and certain internally deployed ones. Off-cycle risk analyses are due when a significantly more capable model is publicly deployed, and within 30 days of identifying a higher-risk internal model.

- **`rsp` · coverage · sec**

  Current:

  > Weight-security tier rises with each ASL — ASL-3 mandates substantially stronger protections against insider threat, exfiltration, and supply-chain attacks. Tied directly to the model's capability profile.

  Proposed:

  > Anthropic commits to maintain or improve the ASL-3 security controls it applies to current models, and plans 'moonshot' security R&D for the automated R&D threshold. The security roughly in line with RAND SL4 that it recommends industry-wide at higher thresholds is not a unilateral commitment.

- **`rsp` · coverage · mit**

  Current:

  > Deployment safeguards by ASL include refusal training, monitoring, abuse detection, and (at higher ASLs) deployment-environment controls. Specific safeguards published for each tier.

  Proposed:

  > Current ASL-3 deployment protections include classifier guards, access controls for trusted users, red-teaming, bug bounties and threat intelligence. For higher thresholds v3 no longer lists required controls; it recommends that developers make a strong argument that risks are contained.

- **`index.html`**

  Current:

  > Anthropic (Responsible Scaling Policy, with AI Safety Levels)

  Proposed:

  > Anthropic (Responsible Scaling Policy, with capability thresholds and periodic Risk Reports)

**Why it matters:** The entry describes the pre-v3 policy: an ASL ladder in which crossing capability evaluations triggers specified safeguards for each tier. v3 (Feb 2026, now v3.4) replaced that structure. The ASL wording also feeds the FAQ answer on lab frameworks, which search engines and LLMs ingest. The entry also implies the RSP is what was scrutinised under SB 53 and the EU Code. Anthropic says its compliance document for both is a separate Frontier Compliance Framework.

**Reasoning:** Each edit is taken from the v3.4 policy text (S-0006); v3.0 (S-0008) already had the same structure. Context: two-tier structure and no unilateral commitment to the industry column (§1, Introduction); ASLs only for present mitigations (Appendix B); Roadmap goals are not hard commitments, and Risk Reports are new (Introduction). The FCF sentence comes from the FCF itself (S-0010#1) and Anthropic's Dec 2025 post (S-0030#1). The RSP also says it handles SB 53-type requirements in separate documents (S-0006#15). Thresholds: the four rows of the §1 table. Evaluations: §3.3 item 3; §1 says evaluations cannot be specified in advance. Timing: §3.1. Security: §1 table, row 1 (ASL-3 controls), the automated R&D row (moonshot security R&D) and the industry column (RAND SL4). Mitigations: §1 table, row 1, and Appendix B. Removed as outdated or unsupported: 'currently up to ASL-3 … each tied to specific capability evaluations and mandatory safeguards'; 'commitments include not deploying at a given ASL until the corresponding mitigations are in place' (pre-v3; v2.0 changelog); 'Subjected to detailed external scrutiny in EU GPAI Code drafting and California SB 53' (not supported by anything inspected, and the compliance document is the FCF); 'autonomous-replication' (replaced by a checkpoint in v2.0, absent from v3); 'pre-training' evaluation timing (absent from v3); 'Specific safeguards published for each tier' (contradicted by Appendix B); and the comparative claim 'Among the most comprehensive timing regimes in any framework' (not checked against other labs).

### P-0013 v1 — Anthropic RSP · Halting: v3 replaced the unconditional pause commitment with competitor-dependent delay commitments

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `fbf2ed18a3d5`

**Linked:** P-0005, P-0010

**Applied together with:** P-0005, P-0006, P-0007, P-0010

**Change**

- **`rsp` · coverage · halt**

  Current:

  > Anthropic commits to pause development or deployment if mitigations are insufficient for the model's ASL. The halting commitment is the most operationally specific in any lab framework.

  Proposed:

  > Since v3.0, Anthropic commits to delay development and deployment in two competitor-dependent scenarios. If it has a significant lead with a highly capable model, it delays until it has a strong argument that catastrophic risk is contained. If all competitors with such models can make that argument, it delays until it matches their risk-reduction posture. Earlier versions committed not to train or deploy models without adequate safeguards, whatever other developers did. Anthropic says it would strongly consider pausing in other cases too.

**Why it matters:** The map says 'Anthropic commits to pause development or deployment if mitigations are insufficient for the model's ASL' and calls this 'the most operationally specific in any lab framework'. That describes the pre-v3 policy. v3 still has delay commitments, but only in Appendix A's competitor-dependent scenarios. This feeds the halting gap summary, which says every lab framework includes halting conditions.

**Reasoning:** From v3.4 Appendix A (scenarios and commitments) and its preamble, where v3.1 added 'would strongly consider pausing … even in cases not covered below'. The Introduction says the previous RSP committed to reduce absolute risk 'without regard to whether other frontier AI developers would do the same'. The v2.0 changelog shows the earlier 'commitment not to train or deploy models unless we have implemented adequate safeguards'. v3.0 already had the same Appendix A commitments (S-0008#1), so the change dates from v3.0. The trial-1 caution 'do not infer that pause commitments were removed' holds: they were made conditional, not removed. Also removed: the comparative claim about other labs, which was not checked. 'Highly capable' is the policy's defined term (crossing the automated AI R&D threshold).

**Evidence**

### P-0014 v1 — US Frontier AI Access EO: describe EO 14409 from its official text (voluntary cyber-capability access; NSA, Treasury and CISA lead, not CAISI)

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `acf23d9552f9`

**Linked:** P-0015

**Change**

- **`us-frontier-access-eo` · link**

  Current:

  > https://www.npr.org/2026/06/02/nx-s1-5844347/ai-safety-trump-executive-order

  Proposed:

  > https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/05/2026-11415/promoting-advanced-artificial-intelligence-innovation-and-security

- **`us-frontier-access-eo` · desc**

  Current:

  > EO signed June 2, 2026. Directs federal agencies to establish a framework for voluntary pre-release access (up to 30 days) by frontier-model developers for national-security review.

  Proposed:

  > EO 14409, signed June 2, 2026. Directs Treasury, NSA and CISA to design a voluntary framework under which developers may give the government access to 'covered frontier models' (designated by the NSA Director via a classified cyber benchmark) for up to 30 days before release to other trusted partners. Rules out mandatory licensing or preclearance.

- **`us-frontier-access-eo` · context**

  Current:

  > Marks a notable shift in the Trump administration's posture — from deregulation (EO 14179) and state preemption (EO 14365) toward asking for federal access to pre-release frontier models. The 30-day voluntary window mirrors the access agreements UK AISI uses; CAISI is positioned to administer reviews. Whether the framework results in a meaningful national-security review process or remains nominal will depend on developer participation.

  Proposed:

  > Marks a notable shift in the Trump administration's posture — from deregulation (EO 14179) and state preemption (EO 14365) toward asking for federal access to pre-release frontier models, though the order itself is scoped to cyber capabilities and rejects 'overly burdensome regulation'. The 30-day voluntary window mirrors the access agreements UK AISI uses. NSA, Treasury and CISA lead; CAISI is not named and NIST is only consulted. Whether the framework results in meaningful federal access will depend on developer participation.

- **`us-frontier-access-eo` · coverage · eval**

  Current:

  > Pre-release access (up to 30 days) could enable systematic federal evaluation of frontier models if developers participate.

  Proposed:

  > Voluntary early access (up to 30 days) to models the NSA designates through a classified cyber-capability benchmark; scoped to cyber capabilities, not general safety evaluation.

- **`us-frontier-access-eo` · coverage · timing**

  Current:

  > 30-day pre-release window; voluntary participation.

  Proposed:

  > Benchmark and framework due within 60 days of the order; access window up to 30 days before release to other trusted partners; participation voluntary.

- **`us-frontier-access-eo` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Federal review mechanism for national-security risks. Departs from prior administration's deregulatory-only posture.

  Proposed:

  > Creates no approval or preclearance power (§3(c)) and no enforceable rights (§5(c)). Also directs a Treasury-led AI cybersecurity clearinghouse and a DOJ enforcement priority on AI-enabled computer crime.

**Why it matters:** The entry's only source is a news article. On the official text, two of its claims are wrong. CAISI does not administer reviews (it is not named; NSA, Treasury and CISA lead, and the NSA Director designates covered models). The order creates no 'review': it sets up voluntary access and expressly rules out preclearance. It also scopes access to cyber capabilities, which the map omits.

**Reasoning:** All new facts come from the Federal Register text, EO 14409, 91 FR 34565 (S-0038), and its FR API record (S-0039): number, title, signing and publication dates, §3 roles, §3(a) classified cyber benchmark and NSA designation, §3(b) voluntary framework and up-to-30-day access before release to other trusted partners, §3(c) no licensing or preclearance, §2(d) clearinghouse, §4 DOJ priority, §5(c) no enforceable rights. The link moves from NPR to the Federal Register document page, matching the map's other EO entries. The context keeps the map's 'notable shift' analysis and the UK AISI comparison (both carried over), adds that the order itself frames things as reducing regulation (§1), and replaces 'CAISI is positioned to administer reviews'.

### P-0016 v1 — EU AI Act: high-risk application dates moved by the Digital Omnibus (Reg. 2026/1744)

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `51eb7ca184a5`

**Change**

- **`eu-aia` · desc**

  Current:

  > In force Aug 2024. GPAI obligations Aug 2025. Most provisions apply Aug 2026; high-risk system rules Aug 2027. Penalties up to €35M or 7% global revenue.

  Proposed:

  > In force Aug 2024. GPAI obligations Aug 2025. Most provisions apply Aug 2026; the 2026 Digital Omnibus (Reg. 2026/1744) moved high-risk rules to Dec 2027 (Annex III) and Aug 2028 (Annex I). Penalties up to €35M or 7% global revenue.

**Why it matters:** The map says high-risk rules apply in Aug 2027. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 Jul 2026, set 2 Dec 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 Aug 2028 for Annex I systems. Even before that, 'Aug 2027' applied only to Annex I.

**Reasoning:** The dates come from the Official Journal text of 2026/1744: Art 1(40)(b), replacing AI Act Art 113(c), and Art 4 for entry into force. The Commission's enforcement page agrees. The other clauses were checked and are unchanged. In force Aug 2024 and GPAI obligations Aug 2025 come from AI Act Art 113 (original OJ). Most provisions apply Aug 2026 is the general date, per Omnibus recital 40. €35M/7% is the top penalty tier (Art 99(3)), which the Commission's penalties passage confirms.

### P-0017 v1 — EU AI Office: GPAI fines are capped at €15M or 3%, not €35M or 7%; enforcement powers apply since Aug 2026

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `b77b6d4a1d68`

**Change**

- **`eu-aia` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Mandatory incident reporting to the EU AI Office for systemic-risk GPAI; market-surveillance authorities handle high-risk systems. The Office can request models, order recalls, and impose fines up to €35M / 7% global revenue.

  Proposed:

  > Mandatory incident reporting to the EU AI Office for systemic-risk GPAI; market-surveillance authorities handle high-risk systems. The Office can request models, order recalls, and fine GPAI providers up to €15M / 3% global revenue.

- **`index.html`**

  Current:

  > impose fines up to €35M or 7% of global revenue, and runs the Scientific Panel of independent experts advising on systemic risk. Full enforcement powers activate in August 2026.

  Proposed:

  > fine GPAI providers up to €15M or 3% of global revenue, and runs the Scientific Panel of independent experts advising on systemic risk. Its enforcement powers have applied since August 2026.

**Why it matters:** Both the eu-aia accountability note and the FAQ answer on the AI Office give the AI Office a fine ceiling of €35M or 7%. That ceiling is for prohibited practices. Fines on GPAI model providers, which the Office enforces, are capped at €15M or 3% (Art 101). The FAQ also still says powers 'activate in August 2026', a date that has passed.

**Reasoning:** From AI Act Art 101(1) (original OJ text, S-0002) and the Commission's enforcement page (S-0043): '€35 million or 7%' for prohibited practices; 'Other breaches, including of the obligations for GPAI models … up to €15 million or 3%'; powers 'apply from 2 August 2026'. The Omnibus (Art 75c(4)) now lets the Office use the Art 99 tiers for AI systems under its new Art 75(1) competence. The highest of those tiers (€35M/7%) is still for prohibited practices only, so 'GPAI providers … €15M / 3%' is the accurate general statement. 'Established January 2024 within DG CNECT' and the Scientific Panel are carried over.

**Evidence**

- **S-0002** Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Official Journal — <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng>
  primary · retrieved 2026-11-09 · access: ok via browser · adopted 2024-06-13, published 2024-07-12, in_force 2024-08-01, applies_from 2026-08-02
  Art 101(1):

### P-0018 v1 — EU GPAI Code: Model Reports every six months, not annual; content marking is not in the GPAI Code

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `57c427d2479d`

**Change**

- **`gpai-cop` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Transparency obligations extend to model documentation, training-data summaries, and copyright disclosures. Signatories report annually; non-signatories must demonstrate AI Act compliance through other means.

  Proposed:

  > Transparency obligations extend to model documentation, training-data summaries, and copyright disclosures. Safety signatories update Model Reports to the AI Office at least every six months for their most capable models; non-signatories must demonstrate AI Act compliance through other means.

- **`gpai-cop` · coverage · mit**

  Current:

  > Deployment mitigations include content marking, refusals, and user-facing transparency. The transparency chapter (separate from safety) governs documentation duties.

  Proposed:

  > Deployment mitigations include input/output filtering, refusals, and staged access. The transparency chapter (separate from safety) governs documentation duties; marking AI-generated content falls under a separate Article 50 code.

**Why it matters:** The map says Code signatories 'report annually'. The Safety and Security chapter requires updated Model Reports to the AI Office at least every six months for a signatory's most capable models. The mitigations note also lists content marking, which the GPAI Code does not require. Marking is an AI Act Article 50 duty, with its own code of practice.

**Reasoning:** From the Safety and Security chapter PDF (S-0044): Measure 7.6 (six-monthly Model Reports) and Measure 5.1 (listed safety mitigations: filtering, refusals, staged access; no marking measure). Watermarks appear only as a post-market monitoring technique. The Article 50 code is described on the Commission's page (S-0045). 'User-facing transparency' is dropped from the mitigations note because nothing inspected supports it as a GPAI Code mitigation.

**Evidence**

- **S-0044** GPAI Code of Practice: Safety and Security chapter (Jul 2025) — <https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/dae/redirection/document/118119>
  primary · retrieved 2026-11-09 · access: ok · published 2025-07-10
  Commitment 7, Measure 7.6:
  > if the model is amongst their respective most capable models available on the market, Signatories will provide the AI Office with an updated Model Report at least every six months.

  _Supports:_ Safety mitigations listed; no content marking

### P-0019 v1 — China AI Law: still a preparatory planning item with no draft; correct the '2025 plan dropped it' claim and add an official source link

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `abfbe2e7035a`

**Change**

- **`cn-ai-law` · link**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > http://www.npc.gov.cn/npc/c2/c30834/202605/P020260511309265804880.pdf

- **`cn-ai-law` · desc**

  Proposed:

  > Comprehensive AI legislation at the planning stage: an unscheduled preparatory item in the NPC Standing Committee's 2025 and 2026 legislative plans; the State Council's 2026 plan calls for accelerating it. No draft has been submitted.

- **`cn-ai-law` · context**

  Current:

  > Would consolidate the patchwork of CAC measures (recommendation algorithms, deep synthesis, generative AI) into a single statute; competing proposals from MOST and CAIC have circulated. The 2025 NPC plan dropped it from preparatory items, so near-term action looks unlikely; in the meantime China is regulating frontier issues through narrower instruments — cybersecurity-law amendments, draft rules on humanlike interactive AI.

  Proposed:

  > Could consolidate the patchwork of CAC measures (recommendation algorithms, deep synthesis, generative AI) into a single statute. The State Council dropped a named AI Law draft from its 2025 plan, then in May 2026 called for accelerating 'comprehensive legislation'; MOST-led drafting of a framework text was under way in late 2025. In the meantime China regulates frontier issues through narrower instruments — a Cybersecurity Law AI article (in force Jan 2026) and CAC rules on humanlike interactive AI (in force Jul 2026).

- **`cn-ai-law` · coverage · thresh**

  Current:

  > Compute thresholds have featured in competing draft proposals from MOST and CAIC; the eventual statute is expected to set capability or compute thresholds, but specifics aren't fixed.

  Proposed:

  > No official draft has been published, so thresholds are not yet defined.

- **`cn-ai-law` · coverage · eval**

  Current:

  > Drafts have signalled risk assessment obligations for high-impact AI systems; details are still being negotiated within the NPC process.

  Proposed:

  > No official draft has been published, so evaluation duties are not yet defined.

- **`cn-ai-law` · coverage · mit**

  Current:

  > Drafts have proposed mitigation duties layered on top of the existing CAC measures, but specifics depend on which competing proposal prevails.

  Proposed:

  > No official draft has been published, so mitigation duties are not yet defined.

- **`cn-ai-law` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Drafts envisage centralised oversight expansion — consolidating algorithm registration, deep-synthesis rules, and generative-AI rules under one statute. Whether this strengthens or duplicates current CAC powers is open.

  Proposed:

  > No official draft has been published, so the oversight structure is not yet defined. Drafting is ministry-led (MOST and others) ahead of any NPC Standing Committee reading.

- **connection `cn-genai` ↔ `cn-ai-law`**

  Current:

  > GenAI Measures will be folded into the AI Law

  Proposed:

  > GenAI Measures could be consolidated into a comprehensive AI law

**Why it matters:** The entry has no source link. It says the law is 'in drafting at NPC' and that 'the 2025 NPC plan dropped it from preparatory items', and its coverage notes describe the contents of 'drafts'. Official sources show there is no published draft. AI legislation is still a preparatory (unscheduled) item in the NPC Standing Committee's 2025 and 2026 plans. It was the State Council's plan that dropped a named 'AI Law draft' in 2025, and its 2026 plan calls for accelerating comprehensive legislation. The 'draft rules on humanlike interactive AI' have since been finalised.

**Reasoning:** Official texts: NPCSC 2026 and 2025 legislative plans (S-0049, S-0050), §(三) preparatory items. State Council plans for 2026 (S-0051), 2025 (S-0052) and 2024 (S-0053, MOJ copy). The NPC committee's Jan 2026 report on AI-law motions (S-0057) covers MOST-led framework drafting. The NPCSC decision amending the Cybersecurity Law adds Art. 20 on AI, adopted 28 Oct 2025 and in force 1 Jan 2026 (S-0054). CAC Order No. 21 on humanlike interactive AI was issued 10 Apr 2026, in force 15 Jul 2026 (S-0056, S-0055). Removed as unsupported: 'Compute thresholds debated', 'competing proposals from MOST and CAIC' (no official source; 'CAIC' is unidentified), the draft-content claims in the coverage notes (no official draft exists), and 'near-term action looks unlikely' (the State Council's 2026 wording is 'accelerate'). The link is the NPCSC 2026 plan PDF, which settles the NPC status. 'Could consolidate…' softens a speculative claim. status 'proposed' and pow 2 are unchanged.

### P-0020 v1 — New entry: EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content (Article 50 marking and labelling)

`addition` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `410d595a202b`

**Change**

- **New entry `eu-genai-code`** — EU AI-generated content code · Layer 5 · jur `eu` · pow 2 · active · https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/code-practice-ai-generated-content

> Voluntary code (final Jun 2026) for the AI Act's Article 50 duties to mark and label AI-generated content; the Commission and AI Board found it adequate in Jul 2026. Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI signed the provider section.

> Two sections: providers commit to machine-readable marking (digitally signed metadata plus imperceptible watermarks) and free detection tools; deployers commit to labelling deepfakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest. Drafted by independent experts under the AI Office, like the GPAI Code, it gives signatories a recognised route to show compliance with duties that apply from Aug 2026; others must show adequate alternatives to national market-surveillance authorities. Unlike the GPAI Code, Meta signed it.

  - _timing_: The underlying Article 50 duties apply from 2 Aug 2026; generative systems already on the market before then have until 2 Dec 2026 for machine-readable marking.
  - _mit_: Providers mark outputs with signed metadata and imperceptible watermarks so they are detectable as AI-generated; deployers label deepfakes and AI-generated text published on matters of public interest. Aimed at deception and misinformation, not catastrophic risk.
  - _acct_: Signatories must offer detection tools free of charge to users, authorities, researchers and media. Adherence is not conclusive proof of compliance; non-signatories must demonstrate adequate alternatives to market-surveillance authorities.

- **new connection `eu-genai-code` ↔ `eu-aia`**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > Code implements the AI Act's Article 50 marking and labelling duties

- **new connection `eu-aio` ↔ `eu-genai-code`**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > AI Office facilitated the drafting by independent experts

**Question for you:** Accept as drafted? Optional extras not included, to keep it minimal: (a) a connection to gpai-cop ('Sibling AI Office code; Meta signed this one but not the GPAI Code'); (b) connections to the lab framework entries of signatories (rsp, prep, meta-faif). Say if you want either.

**Why it matters:** A second AI Act code of practice, adopted in July 2026, that the map does not cover. It shapes how every major generative AI provider, including the frontier labs on the map, marks and enables detection of model outputs in the EU. The maintainer asked for it to be drafted (2026-10-10).

**Reasoning:** Meets RUBRIC §1. It is identifiable (published code text, S-0060). It is material: contextual under SCOPE §C, because it governs deployment-stage marking by GPAI and generative AI providers rather than catastrophic risk. It is attributable: drawn up under the AI Office and assessed as adequate by the Commission and AI Board (S-0046). Layer 5, jur eu, pow 2 and status active mirror gpai-cop, the map's other AI Office code. pow 2 follows RUBRIC §4 ('voluntary government codes'). Every fact comes from Commission pages or the code itself: final publication 10 Jun 2026 (S-0059); adequacy 8 and 9 Jul 2026, and adherence not conclusive proof (S-0046); two sections and non-signatories assessed by market surveillance (S-0045); signed metadata and watermarking (S-0060, Measure 1.1); free detection solution for users, authorities, researchers and media (S-0060, Measure 2.1). Application dates come from the AI Act as amended (S-0041, Art 111(4); S-0045). Section 1 signatories are named by the Commission (S-0058). Meta's absence from the GPAI Code list is from S-0003. Coverage notes are limited to the three METR elements the code actually addresses.

The press release also says firms would publish frameworks 'where they have not done so already' (seoulpr#p3). OpenAI and Google are on the signatory list (seoul#p1). Wording follows P-0008.

### P-0026 v2 — Delhi commitments: two commitments on usage data and multilingual evaluation; no risk obligations; 13 signatories, fewer than Seoul

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v2, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `4df8cface848`

_Revised from v1: wording changed, so it needs a fresh decision._

**Change**

- **`delhi-commit` · desc**

  Current:

  > New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments (Feb 2026). 13 frontier developers; broader than Seoul.

  Proposed:

  > New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments (Feb 2026). 13 signatories, including four India-based developers; commitments on AI-usage data and multilingual evaluation.

- **`delhi-commit` · context**

  Current:

  > Extends the Seoul template to cover beneficial use cases — energy efficiency, healthcare, public services — alongside risk obligations. Signatory base broader than Seoul (added Indian and global-south firms) but commitments are weaker on concrete capability thresholds. Reflects the Delhi summit's 'impact' rather than 'safety' framing.

  Proposed:

  > Unlike Seoul, contains no thresholds or risk-mitigation commitments. Signatories commit to publish, by the next AI Summit, statistics from anonymised usage data to inform policy on jobs and skills, and to evaluate multilingual capabilities with local ecosystems; progress is to be reported through mechanisms such as the Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework. Adds India-based developers (including Sarvam AI and BharatGen) not in Seoul. Reflects the Delhi summit's 'impact' rather than 'safety' framing.

- **`delhi-commit` · coverage · mit**

  Current:

  > Inclusive deployment alongside risk obligations — signatories commit to consider beneficial use cases (energy, healthcare, public services) as well as risk mitigation. Reflects the Delhi summit's 'impact' rather than safety framing.

  Proposed:

  > _(absent)_

- **`delhi-commit` · coverage · eval**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > Signatories commit to evaluate multilingual capabilities on a subset of languages and cultural contexts and to collaborate with local ecosystems on evaluations for under-represented languages. A stretch: about performance across languages, not dangerous capabilities.

- **`delhi-commit` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Public commitments by 13 frontier developers, including Indian and global-south firms not represented in Seoul. Broader signatory base, weaker on concrete capability thresholds than Seoul.

  Proposed:

  > Public commitments by 13 signatories, including India-based developers not in Seoul (including Sarvam AI and BharatGen). Signatories commit to publish usage statistics by the next summit and, where practicable, to report progress through the Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework. No enforcement.

**Why it matters:** The entry describes commitments the text does not contain. The two-page text has two commitments: publish usage statistics and strengthen multilingual evaluation. There are no risk obligations and nothing on energy, healthcare or public services. With 13 signatories it is smaller than Seoul (20), not broader.

**Reasoning:** Text and signee list (as on 23 Feb 2026) from the summit's outcome document (delhi#p1–p6; observation delhi#p7). PIB release of 19 Feb 2026 for the announcement and the Indian firms (pib#p1–p3). Seoul's count from seoul#p1–p2. The mitigation coverage is removed because the text has no mitigation commitment (delhi#p7). Evaluation coverage is added as a marked stretch (delhi#p4–p5). The accountability note now cites the reporting route (delhi#p1, delhi#p3). Revised before review: the official signee list spells two India-based signees 'Gynani.ai' and 'Socket Labs' (S-0069#6), so the entry names only the two whose spelling the list confirms.

### P-0030 v1 — GPAI Code thresholds: signatories define capability-based risk tiers; the 10^25 FLOP presumption sets scope, not tiers

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `05ee601223d9`

**Change**

- **`gpai-cop` · coverage · thresh**

  Current:

  > The safety/security chapter calls for capability thresholds tied to systemic risks, mirroring the EU AI Act's 10²⁵ FLOPs trigger. Concrete threshold-setting is left to signatory firms.

  Proposed:

  > The safety/security chapter requires measurable systemic-risk tiers defined in terms of model capabilities for each identified risk (Measure 4.1). The AI Act's 10²⁵ FLOP presumption decides which models the chapter covers, not where the tiers sit; concrete threshold-setting is left to signatory firms.

**Why it matters:** The note says the Code's thresholds mirror the AI Act's 10^25 FLOP trigger. They do not. The FLOP figure is the Act's presumption of systemic risk, which decides who is covered. The Code's thresholds are capability-based risk tiers that each signatory defines.

**Reasoning:** Measure 4.1 (gpaiss#p1): tiers 'defined in terms of model capabilities', measurable, at least one not yet reached. The 10^25 FLOP presumption is Article 51 classification (gpaiqa#p1, gpaiactqa#p1). The Code does not address the classification thresholds (gpaiactqa#p2). The last clause of the current note is kept.

**Evidence**

- **S-0044** GPAI Code of Practice: Safety and Security chapter (Jul 2025) — <https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/dae/redirection/document/118119>
  primary · retrieved 2026-11-09 · access: ok · published 2025-07-10
  Commitment 4, Measure 4.1:
  > for each identified systemic risk (pursuant to Measure 2.1), at least: (a) define appropriate systemic risk tiers that: (i) are defined in terms of model capabilities, and may additionally incorporate model propensities, risk estimates, and/or other suitable metrics; (ii) are measurable; and (iii) comprise at least one systemic risk tier that has not been reached by the model
  _Supports:_ signatory-defined capability tiers
- **S-0089** European Commission: Questions and answers on the Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI — <https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/questions-and-answers-code-practice-general-purpose-ai>
  primary · retrieved 2026-11-09 · access: ok
  What is the Code:
  > The AI Act currently presumes that models trained with a cumulative amount of compute greater than 10^25 floating-point operations possess high-impact capabilities.
  _Supports:_ 10^25 FLOP presumption of high-impact capabilities
- **S-0091** European Commission: General-Purpose AI Models in the AI Act – Q&A — <https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/general-purpose-ai-models-ai-act-questions-answers>
  primary · retrieved 2026-11-09 · access: ok
  Systemic risk:
  > the AI Act lays down a threshold of 10^ 25 floating-point operations (FLOP) used for training the model (Article 51(1)(a) and (2) AI Act).
  _Supports:_ Art 51 FLOP threshold
