  > updating the criteria or thresholds for classifying a general-purpose AI model as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk (Article 51)
  _Supports:_ Code does not set classification thresholds

**Uncertainty:** None material.

### P-0031 v1 — GPAI Code elicitation: state-of-the-art elicitation and external evaluation are required; red-teaming is an example method

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `657d0302f0b6`

Among the strongest elicitation requirements in any non-binding instrument.

### P-0032 v1 — GPAI Code security: no supply-chain measures; protections cover weights, interfaces and insider threats

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: medium · change-hash `9454839f9d87`

**Change**

- **`gpai-cop` · coverage · sec**

  Current:

  > Model security obligations cover weight protection, secure deployment infrastructure, and supply-chain controls. Bridges Article 55 of the EU AI Act with concrete operational expectations.

  Proposed:

  > Model security obligations cover protection of unreleased model parameters, hardened interfaces, physical infrastructure and insider threats, with external security reviews and red-teaming as assurance (Commitment 6, Appendix 4). Bridges Article 55 of the EU AI Act with concrete operational expectations.

**Why it matters:** The note lists 'supply-chain controls', which the security chapter does not contain. It also omits insider-threat measures, which have their own appendix.

**Reasoning:** Commitment 6 (gpaiss#p6); Appendix 4.2 and 4.4 (gpaiss#p7, gpaiss#p8); text search for 'supply' found nothing (gpaiss#p9). Interface hardening and security assurance are Appendix 4.3 and 4.5 (gpaiss#p9).

### P-0033 v1 — GPAI Code updates: the AI Office reviews the Code at least every two years

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `97572f8681e4`

**Change**

- **`gpai-cop` · coverage · update**

  Current:

  > Periodic Code of Practice revisions handled by independent experts under the AI Office. The Code is the operational layer that updates faster than the underlying regulation.

  Proposed:

  > The AI Office reviews the Code at least every two years and may facilitate formal updates in response to technology, risk or enforcement experience; signatories are invited to sign updated versions. The Code is the operational layer that updates faster than the underlying regulation.

**Why it matters:** The note says revisions are 'handled by independent experts under the AI Office'. The Commission says the AI Office reviews the Code at least every two years and facilitates updates. Independent experts drafted the 2025 text; the sources inspected give them no standing role in revisions.

**Reasoning:** Commission Q&A (gpaiqa#p3, last updated 20 Jul 2026); signing Q&A (gpaisignqa#p1, gpaisignqa#p2). The Code has been unchanged since 10 Jul 2025 (gpaisig#p1).

### P-0035 v1 — FMF: members signed an information-sharing agreement (Mar 2025); FMF files public comments but does not lobby

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: medium · change-hash `f47abdfa0ef3`

**Change**

- **`fmf` · context**

  Current:

  > Funds safety research grants, coordinates evaluation methodology between member labs, and convenes shared technical forums. Doesn't impose obligations on members or speak with one voice in policy debates. Some critics argue it is too closely held by its member labs; others that its remit is too narrow to drive policy change. The substantive contribution is in the research outputs, not the political coordination.

  Proposed:

  > Funds safety research grants, coordinates evaluation methodology between member labs, and convenes shared technical forums. Since Mar 2025 all members have signed a voluntary agreement to share information on frontier-AI vulnerabilities, threats and capabilities of concern; beyond that it imposes no obligations and does not lobby. Some critics argue it is too closely held by its member labs; others that its remit is too narrow to drive policy change. The substantive contribution is in the research outputs, not the political coordination.

- **`fmf` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Industry coordination on safety practice — funds research grants, convenes shared technical forums, publishes cross-lab perspectives. Doesn't speak with one voice in policy debates or impose obligations on members.

  Proposed:

  > Industry coordination on safety practice — funds research grants, convenes shared technical forums, publishes cross-lab perspectives, and runs a members' information-sharing agreement on threats and vulnerabilities (Mar 2025). Does not lobby or impose other obligations on members.

**Why it matters:** The entry says the FMF imposes no obligations on members. Since March 2025 every member has signed an information-sharing agreement, which the FMF reported in Feb 2026 is in use. This is the forum's one cross-firm commitment. 'Doesn't speak with one voice in policy debates' is also hard to square with its own public comments and congressional testimony; its stated position is that it does not lobby.

**Reasoning:** Agreement: fmfisa#p1, fmfisa#p2; in use: fmfisp#p1, fmfisp#p2; dated 28 Mar 2025 (fmfpubs#p6). No lobbying: fmfabout#p1. Public comments and testimony in 2026: fmfpubs#p4, fmfpubs#p5. Grants: fmfasf#p1.

### P-0036 v1 — PAI: has a foundation-model deployment framework (2023) and a 2026 report tracking providers

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: medium · change-hash `8056409cfae7`

**Change**

- **`pai` · context**

  Current:

  > Member-driven org with academics, NGOs, media, and tech firms; produces guidance on synthetic media disclosure, AI in journalism, AI workforce impacts. Pre-dates the frontier-AI debate and hasn't fully repositioned to it. Most influential as a multistakeholder venue for non-technical issues that frontier-only forums (FMF, AISI Network) skip.

  Proposed:

  > Member-driven org with academics, NGOs, media, and tech firms; produces guidance on synthetic media disclosure, AI in journalism, AI workforce impacts. Pre-dates the frontier-AI debate; its frontier-relevant work is the 2023 Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment and a 2026 report tracking 13 organisations' public disclosure of foundation-model impacts. Most influential as a multistakeholder venue for non-technical issues that frontier-only forums (FMF, AISI Network) skip.

**Why it matters:** The entry says PAI 'hasn't fully repositioned' to frontier AI without mentioning its frontier-model work. That work is the Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment (2023), a framework for model providers, and a 2026 report tracking 13 organisations against it.

**Reasoning:** The guidance is described on PAI's home page (paihome#p1). The 2026 report covers 13 organisations and builds on the 2023 guidance (paitr#p1).

**Evidence**

It builds on our 2023 Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment and our 2025 progress-tracking methodology
  _Supports:_ 2026 report: 13 organisations, builds on 2023 guidance

(synthetic media and workforce checked: paihome#p2, paihome#p3); context: 'Most influential as a multistakeholder venue for non-technical issues that frontier-only forums (FMF, AISI Network) skip.'

**Uncertainty:** Whether this amounts to 'repositioning' is a judgment; the edit replaces the judgment with the facts. 'AI in journalism' guidance was not checked and is carried over.

### P-0037 v1 — OpenAI Preparedness: describe v2 (Apr 2025), not the 2023 beta

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `99247eeda875`

**Change**

- **`prep` · desc**

  Current:

  > Preparedness Framework. Tracked categories (cyber, CBRN, autonomy, persuasion). 2025 revisions tightened bio thresholds.

  Proposed:

  > Preparedness Framework v2 (Apr 2025). Tracked categories (bio/chem, cyber, AI self-improvement) with High and Critical thresholds; persuasion moved out of the framework.

- **`prep` · context**

  Current:

  > Tracks four risk categories (cyber, CBRN, autonomy, persuasion) at low/medium/high/critical levels; deployment requires reaching specific thresholds and implementing graduated mitigations. Decisions reviewed by an internal Safety Advisory Group that escalates to the board. The 2025 revisions reframed the persuasion category and lowered the bio-risk threshold after CBRN evaluation findings. May 2026 added a separate Frontier Governance Framework mapping OpenAI's safety practices to California SB 53 and the EU GPAI Code — a companion governance layer alongside the Preparedness Framework.

  Proposed:

  > Tracks three categories (biological and chemical, cybersecurity, AI self-improvement) against High and Critical capability thresholds; Research Categories (e.g. long-range autonomy, sandbagging, nuclear and radiological) are studied but not yet tracked. High capability requires safeguards that sufficiently minimise severe risk before deployment; Critical also requires them during development. An internal Safety Advisory Group recommends, OpenAI Leadership decides, and the board's Safety and Security Committee oversees. In September 2026 OpenAI designated GPT-6 Astra its first model at the Critical cybersecurity level. May 2026 added a separate Frontier Governance Framework mapping OpenAI's safety practices to California SB 53 and the EU GPAI Code — a companion governance layer alongside the Preparedness Framework.

- **`prep` · coverage · thresh**

  Current:

  > Tracks four risk categories (cyber, CBRN, autonomy, persuasion) at low/medium/high/critical levels; deployment requires specific thresholds and graduated mitigations. Different threshold structure from Anthropic's ASLs — category × level matrix rather than single-axis tier.

  Proposed:

  > Three Tracked Categories (bio/chem, cyber, AI self-improvement), each with High and Critical capability thresholds; v2 dropped the low and medium levels. Different threshold structure from Anthropic's ASLs — category × level matrix rather than single-axis tier.

- **`prep` · coverage · eval**

  Current:

  > Evaluations against tracked categories run pre-deployment and ongoing; methodology disclosed in the framework and updated 2024–2025. External evaluators (METR, Apollo) participate.

  Proposed:

  > Automated scalable evaluations on every covered model before deployment, validated by expert-led deep dives; methodology set out in the framework (v2, 2025). External evaluators (METR, Apollo, UK AISI) participate.

- **`prep` · coverage · elicit**

  Current:

  > Capability elicitation through adversarial scaffolding, red-teaming, and agentic deployment is built into the evaluation protocols. Apollo's scheming research has shaped the autonomy category specifically.

  Proposed:

  > Evaluations aim to approximate the high end of elicitation by threat actors — highest-capability settings, a model variant with negligible safety refusals, the best available scaffolds, fine-tuning if weights will be released — and treat results as a lower bound. Sandbagging is a Research Category.

- **`prep` · coverage · sec**

  Current:

  > Weight security obligations scale with risk level; high/critical-risk models trigger enhanced protections. Specific tier definitions disclosed in the framework.

  Proposed:

  > Security controls meeting a High standard (threat modelling, defence in depth, access management and related practices) are required for High-capability models; the framework says a Critical standard is still to be specified.

- **`prep` · coverage · mit**

  Current:

  > Deployment safeguards graduated by risk level — refusals, monitoring, agentic controls, deployment-environment restrictions. Critical-risk gates production deployment outright.

  Proposed:

  > Safeguards against malicious users (refusal training, usage monitoring, trust-based access) and against misaligned models (alignment, oversight, restricted system architecture), documented in Safeguards Reports. High-capability models deploy only once safeguards sufficiently minimise severe risk.

- **`prep` · coverage · halt**

  Current:

  > High and critical risk levels gate deployment; OpenAI commits not to ship at those levels until mitigations reduce risk to medium or below. Explicit halting commitment subject to internal Safety Advisory Group review.

  Proposed:

  > Commits not to deploy High-capability models until safeguards sufficiently minimise the associated severe risk, and for Critical capability to halt further development until safeguards and security controls meeting a Critical standard are specified. May adjust safeguards if a rival ships a comparable system without them, but only with public acknowledgement and while staying more protective.

- **`prep` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Internal Safety Advisory Group reviews evaluations and escalates to the board for high/critical-risk decisions. External transparency is through the published framework rather than reporting to a regulator.

  Proposed:

  > Safety Advisory Group reviews Capabilities and Safeguards Reports and recommends; OpenAI Leadership makes final decisions, overseen by the board's Safety and Security Committee, which can reverse them. Results are published with system cards; the separate Frontier Governance Framework covers incident reporting to authorities under SB 53 and the EU Code.

- **`prep` · coverage · update**

  Current:

  > Framework updated in 2024 and 2025; the 2025 revision reframed the persuasion category and lowered the bio-risk threshold after CBRN evaluation findings.

  Proposed:

  > Beta Dec 2023; v2 Apr 2025 dropped persuasion and the low/medium levels, split model autonomy and added Research Categories. Commits to review the framework at least once a year.

**Why it matters:** The entry describes the December 2023 beta (four categories including persuasion, low-to-critical scale, "medium or below" deployment rule, board escalation). OpenAI replaced it in April 2025; readers comparing labs get OpenAI's current commitments wrong, including its halting language and governance. Astra (Sep 2026) is the first model OpenAI designated Critical.

**Reasoning:** Preparedness Framework v2 (still the version OpenAI links from its Sep 2026 Astra post and system card) sets three Tracked Categories, High/Critical thresholds, moves persuasion out, commits to halt further development at Critical until a Critical standard exists, and sets SAG → Leadership → board SSC governance. The beta is the source of the current wording. The "2025 revisions tightened/lowered bio thresholds" claim has no support in v2's change log. Evaluator participation comes from the GPT-5.6 (METR) and GPT-6 Astra (Apollo, UK AISI) system cards.

### P-0038 v1 — GDM Frontier Safety Framework: correct versions and describe v3.1

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `321c05de044e`

**Change**

- **`fsf` · desc**

  Current:

  > Critical Capability Levels and mitigations. v3 (April 2026) is the current version; v2 (2024) added explicit deceptive-alignment evaluations.

  Proposed:

  > Critical Capability Levels and mitigations. v3.1 (17 Apr 2026) is the current version and added lower Tracked Capability Levels; v2 (Feb 2025) added a deceptive-alignment approach.

- **`fsf` · context**

  Current:

  > Defines Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) across cyber-offence, biorisk, ML R&D, and deceptive-alignment domains; each CCL maps to concrete security and deployment mitigations. v2 (2024) added explicit deceptive-alignment evaluations after Apollo Research findings; subsequent updates extended the autonomous-task evaluation strand. Less prescriptive than Anthropic's RSP on halting commitments — relies more on internal review than published red-lines.

  Proposed:

  > Defines Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) in CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation and ML R&D, with lower Tracked Capability Levels (TCLs) for CBRN and for misalignment (stealth and situational awareness); each CCL carries a recommended security level and a deployment-mitigation process that needs a safety case. v2 (Feb 2025) added a deceptive-alignment approach; v3 (Sep 2025) added harmful manipulation; v3.1 (Apr 2026) folded misalignment into a combined ML R&D and misalignment domain. Less prescriptive than Anthropic's RSP on halting commitments — relies more on internal review than published red-lines.

- **`fsf` · coverage · thresh**

  Current:

  > Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) defined across cyber-offence, biorisk, ML R&D, and deceptive-alignment domains. Capability-tier framing — somewhere between Anthropic's ASLs and OpenAI's category × level matrix.

  Proposed:

  > Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) in CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation and ML R&D, plus lower Tracked Capability Levels (CBRN; stealth and situational awareness) added in v3.1. Capability-tier framing — somewhere between Anthropic's ASLs and OpenAI's category × level matrix.

- **`fsf` · coverage · elicit**

  Current:

  > v2 (2024) added explicit deceptive-alignment evaluations after Apollo Research findings — among the first lab frameworks to formally adopt scheming evaluations as a capability-elicitation strand.

  Proposed:

  > Evaluations apply scaffolding, inference compute and other augmentations to assess the systems likely to be built on the model; per-model FSF reports describe agentic scaffolding and sandbagging checks. v2 (Feb 2025) added instrumental-reasoning (deceptive-alignment) levels, now the stealth and situational awareness TCL.

- **`fsf` · coverage · timing**

  Current:

  > Evaluations run periodically rather than at strict pre-training/pre-deployment milestones. Less granular timing structure than Anthropic's RSP.

  Proposed:

  > Critical capability assessment before a model's first external deployment; material-capability-change assessments on checkpoints after post-training runs decide whether later versions need a new one. Alert thresholds flag approach to a CCL between assessments.

- **`fsf` · coverage · sec**

  Current:

  > Security mitigations per CCL — protections scale with the capability profile. Specifics published in the framework but less granular than Anthropic's tier system.

  Proposed:

  > Recommended security level per CCL, aligned with RAND levels: Security Level 2+ (SL2 plus insider-threat and non-state-actor measures) for CBRN, cyber and harmful manipulation; SL3 and SL4 for the ML R&D CCLs. Framed as the minimum the field should apply.

- **`fsf` · coverage · halt**

  Current:

  > Halts at critical levels are committed pending mitigation review — but the halting trigger is less prescriptive than Anthropic's RSP, relying more on internal review than published red-lines.

  Proposed:

  > Commits that external deployments (and, for ML R&D and misalignment levels, high-risk internal deployments) proceed only after a governance function finds residual risk acceptable, with a safety case once a CCL is reached; for misuse levels this applies to external deployment, not further development. Relies more on internal review than published red-lines.

- **`fsf` · coverage · update**

  Current:

  > v2 (2024) added deceptive-alignment evaluations after Apollo Research findings; v3 (April 2026) extended the autonomous-task evaluation strand. Update cadence less formalised than Anthropic's RSP.

  Proposed:

  > v1 May 2024; v2 Feb 2025 (security levels, deceptive-alignment approach); v3 Sep 2025 (harmful manipulation, ML R&D protocols); v3.1 Apr 2026 (TCLs, SL2+, governance section). Commits to review at least once a year.

**Why it matters:** The entry dates v2 to 2024 and calls the April 2026 text "v3"; v3 was September 2025 and April 2026 is v3.1. It lists a biorisk/deceptive-alignment domain set that no longer exists, attributes v2 to Apollo findings with no support, and describes a halting commitment and timing structure that v3.1 does not contain.

**Reasoning:** FSF v3.1 (17 Apr 2026) lists its version history, its four risk domains, TCLs, security levels, pre-first-deployment assessments, and deployment gates. DeepMind's Feb 2025 post introduces the deceptive-alignment approach without mentioning Apollo. v3.1 contains no "halt", "pause", "on hold" or "stop"; its gates are deployment conditions, written here as commitments.

### P-0039 v1 — Meta framework: describe v2 thresholds and the change from "stop" to "develop with mitigations"

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `3102d059d08f`

**Change**

- **`meta-faif` · context**

  Current:

  > Two-tier risk classification: high-risk released with mitigations, critical-risk not released at all until mitigations reduce the risk to high. Explicit commitment not to ship critical-risk models — the headline differentiator with xAI's framework. The only major US lab to refuse the EU GPAI Code, putting Meta's compliance route under the AI Act in question.

  Proposed:

  > Risk thresholds (critical, high, moderate or lower) across chemical and biological, cyber and, since v2, loss of control. v2 replaced "stop" at the critical threshold with "develop with mitigations": Meta commits to deploy high- or critical-threshold models only once validated mitigations reduce risk to that of a moderate-or-lower model, and to continue developing a critical-threshold model only if catastrophic risks are within acceptable levels. The only major US lab to refuse the EU GPAI Code, putting Meta's compliance route under the AI Act in question.

- **`meta-faif` · coverage · thresh**

  Current:

  > Two-tier classification — high-risk (released with mitigations) and critical-risk (not released until mitigations reduce risk to high). Coarser than Anthropic's ASLs or OpenAI's category × level matrix.

  Proposed:

  > Three thresholds — critical, high, moderate or lower — set by whether a model would substantially contribute to a threat scenario for a catastrophic outcome in chemical and biological, cyber or loss-of-control risk. Coarser than Anthropic's ASLs or OpenAI's category × level matrix.

- **`meta-faif` · coverage · eval**

  Current:

  > Evaluations against the two risk tiers; less methodological detail published than peers. External evaluator participation limited.

  Proposed:

  > Risk assessments against the thresholds before release, with a published preparedness report for each closed or open Frontier AI release describing evaluations, methodology and evaluator access. External experts join threat modelling where relevant.

- **`meta-faif` · coverage · elicit**

  Current:

  > Adversarial testing performed pre-deployment; specifics not heavily disclosed. Less developed than the elicitation work in RSP, Preparedness, or FSF.

  Proposed:

  > Commits to assess with maximum elicitation in mind — evaluating the model as part of a system with the scaffolding and tooling available for the proposed deployment — to capture the upper bound of risk.

- **`meta-faif` · coverage · timing**

  Current:

  > Pre-deployment evaluation; ongoing monitoring at the tier level. Update cadence and trigger conditions not heavily specified.

  Proposed:

  > Assessments during development and before release; a new preparedness report is triggered by a newly pre-trained model, a large compute increase or changes that materially increase relevant capabilities, with preliminary assessments before controlled deployments.

- **`meta-faif` · coverage · mit**

  Current:

  > Deployment mitigations layered onto release — high-risk models ship with mitigations; critical-risk models don't ship at all. Mitigation specifics discretionary.

  Proposed:

  > Mitigations required before deployment at the high threshold and before further development at the critical threshold, validated to reduce risk to moderate or lower; specific measures adapt to each scenario.

- **`meta-faif` · coverage · halt**

  Current:

  > Explicit commitment not to ship critical-risk models — the headline differentiator from xAI's framework. Halting trigger tied to the binary tier rather than graduated capabilities.

  Proposed:

  > v2 (Apr 2026) changed the critical threshold from "stop" to "develop with mitigations": Meta commits to continue development only if catastrophic risks are within acceptable levels and to deploy only after validated mitigations reduce risk to moderate or lower.

- **`meta-faif` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Internal review; thinner external accountability surface than peers. Refused to sign the EU GPAI Code, putting Meta's compliance route under the AI Act in question.

  Proposed:

  > Chief AI Officer oversees the process and approves deployments, supported by a Director of Alignment and Risk; the Board oversees regulatory compliance; preparedness reports are published per release, with whistleblower and non-compliance reporting. Refused to sign the EU GPAI Code, putting Meta's compliance route under the AI Act in question.

- **`meta-faif` · coverage · update**

  Current:

  > Released Feb 2025 after pressure; revision schedule not publicly committed. Among the slowest-evolving lab frameworks.

  Proposed:

  > Released Feb 2025; v2 (Apr 2026) renamed it Advanced AI Scaling Framework and revised thresholds, domains and governance. Commits to review at least annually.

**Why it matters:** The entry still describes "critical-risk not released at all" as Meta's headline commitment. Meta's v2 (7 Apr 2026) explicitly changed the critical measure from "Stop" to "Develop with Mitigations", added loss of control and named accountable officers, so the map overstates Meta's halting commitment and understates its new transparency commitments.

**Reasoning:** Meta's v2 PDF (linked from the map entry) has a change log recording each change, the three-threshold table, the development and deployment conditions, the governance roles, preparedness-report triggers, maximum-elicitation language and the annual review commitment. The EC signatory list still omits Meta.

### P-0041 v1 — xAI framework: current edition (30 Jun 2026), lifecycle timing and acceptance commitment

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `875995b9d69d`

**Change**

- **`xai-rmf` · desc**

  Current:

  > Published Feb 2025 after delay. Thinner than peers. xAI suing Colorado over AI Act.

  Proposed:

  > Draft Feb 2025; final Risk Management Framework Aug 2025, renamed Frontier AI Framework Dec 2025; current edition effective 30 Jun 2026. Thinner than peers. xAI suing Colorado over AI Act.

- **`xai-rmf` · context**

  Current:

  > Quantitative-benchmark approach to capability evaluation (chosen benchmarks rather than red-lined capability thresholds), with internal review processes. Independent reviews of frontier risk-management frameworks have flagged the narrow scope of risk tolerances and limited halting commitments as gaps. xAI's litigation against Colorado SB 24-205 makes it the most visible lab opponent of state-level AI regulation in the US.

  Proposed:

  > Earlier editions set benchmark-based acceptance criteria (e.g. answering under 1 in 20 restricted bio/chem queries; MASK dishonesty under 1 in 2); the 30 Jun 2026 edition is restructured along the EU GPAI Code's Safety and Security Chapter, covering CBRN, offensive cyber, loss of control and harmful manipulation, and states no numeric criteria. Independent reviews of frontier risk-management frameworks have flagged the narrow scope of risk tolerances and limited halting commitments as gaps. xAI's litigation against Colorado SB 24-205 makes it the most visible lab opponent of state-level AI regulation in the US.

- **`xai-rmf` · coverage · thresh**

  Current:

  > Quantitative-benchmark approach — emphasises specific benchmark scores (e.g., bio/chem answer rates) rather than red-lined capability thresholds. Independent reviews of frontier risk-management frameworks have flagged the narrow scope and absence of well-defined risk tolerances as gaps.

  Proposed:

  > Risk acceptance by reviewing systemic-risk tiers per domain (CBRN, offensive cyber, loss of control, harmful manipulation) using public and internal benchmarks; the Jun 2026 edition states no numeric criteria, where earlier editions set benchmark limits such as answering under 1 in 20 restricted bio/chem queries. Independent reviews of frontier risk-management frameworks have flagged the narrow scope and absence of well-defined risk tolerances as gaps.

- **`xai-rmf` · coverage · timing**

  Current:

  > Pre-deployment evaluation only; ongoing monitoring or re-evaluation triggers not heavily specified. Less comprehensive lifecycle coverage than peers.

  Proposed:

  > Risk management across the model lifecycle, including post-market monitoring; a full systemic risk assessment at least yearly, with smaller evaluations at triggers such as an updated model, a serious incident or materially increased risk.

- **`xai-rmf` · coverage · halt**

  Current:

  > Limited halting commitments — independent analyses have flagged the absence of clear pause triggers. Distinguishes xAI from Meta's explicit critical-risk halt.

  Proposed:

  > Commits to proceed with development, market release or use only if systemic risks are determined acceptable, and may temporarily shut down a system during an incident; defines no capability-specific pause triggers. Independent analyses have flagged the absence of clear pause triggers.

- **`xai-rmf` · coverage · update**

  Current:

  > Framework released after delay (Feb 2025); revision schedule not publicly committed.

  Proposed:

  > Draft Feb 2025 promised an update within three months; final RMF Aug 2025, renamed Frontier AI Framework Dec 2025 and revised again Jun 2026 without a published change log. Commits to periodic review.

**Why it matters:** The entry dates xAI's framework to February 2025 (a draft) and describes only its benchmark-threshold approach. xAI has since issued three editions; the current one (effective 30 Jun 2026) follows the EU Code's Safety and Security Chapter, adds lifecycle and annual-assessment commitments, and drops the numeric criteria. The halt note also compares xAI with a Meta "critical-risk halt" that Meta revised in April 2026.

**Reasoning:** The four xAI PDFs (Feb 2025 draft, Aug 2025 RMF, Dec 2025 FAIF, Jun 2026 FAIF) and the x.ai/safety page show the sequence and current text; the DOJ press release confirms xAI sued over SB24-205 on 9 Apr 2026.

  Current:

  > Members: UK, US/CAISI, EU AI Office, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Canada, France INESIA, Australia, Kenya. Renamed Dec 2025 (San Diego convening) to "International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science."

  Proposed:

- **`oecd` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Transparency, explainability, and accountability are three of the five values-based principles. Adopting countries are encouraged to embed them in domestic frameworks rather than report on them.

  Proposed:

  > Transparency and explainability, and accountability, are two of the five values-based principles. Adopting countries are encouraged to embed them in domestic frameworks rather than report on them.

### P-0054 v1 — New entry: UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and Global Dialogue on AI Governance

`addition` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: medium · change-hash `c6ae155f8cbc`

**Change**

- **New entry `un-ai`** — UN AI Panel & Dialogue · Layer 1 · jur `mu` · pow 1 · active · https://www.un.org/independent-international-scientific-panel-ai/en

> UN General Assembly resolution 79/325 (Aug 2025) created a 40-member Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and an annual Global Dialogue on AI Governance. The Panel (co-chairs Yoshua Bengio, Maria Ressa) issued its Preliminary Report in Jul 2026 and a brief on AI agents and loss of control in Sep 2026; the first Dialogue met in Geneva in Jul 2026.

> The UN's universal-membership counterpart to the International AI Safety Report and the summit series. The Panel's annual report is policy-relevant but non-prescriptive and is presented at the Dialogue, a platform whose topics include safe, secure and trustworthy AI, human rights and interoperable governance; its outcomes are co-chairs' summaries, not negotiated texts. Non-military domain only. The Sep 2026 brief, on AI agents that breached Hugging Face's systems while under evaluation at OpenAI, put loss-of-control risk on the UN agenda.

  - _eval_: Synthesises scientific evidence on AI capabilities, risks and safeguards rather than testing models itself; its first thematic brief assessed a real incident involving AI agents under evaluation.
  - _acct_: Annual report presented to governments at the Global Dialogue, plus up to two updates a year to the General Assembly plenary. No enforcement: accountability through shared evidence and public debate.
  - _update_: One annual report plus thematic briefs as the Panel deems necessary; the Dialogue meets annually, alternating between Geneva and New York (next: New York, May 2027).

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > AISR positions itself as complementary to the UN Panel; Bengio chairs both

- **new connection `un-ai` ↔ `unesco`**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > UNESCO co-coordinates the Global Dialogue's joint secretariat with ITU

- **new connection `ai-summits` ↔ `un-ai`**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > Paris summit statement reaffirmed support for launching the Panel and Dialogue

**Why it matters:** A UN body with an adopted General Assembly mandate that now issues frontier-relevant scientific assessments, including a Sep 2026 brief on AI-agent misalignment and loss of control. The Global Dialogue is the only universal-membership intergovernmental forum on AI governance. SCOPE B3 allows a UN body as a proposed addition when it has an adopted mandate bearing on frontier/GPAI governance.

**Reasoning:** RUBRIC §1. Identifiable: A/RES/79/325 of 26 Aug 2025. Material: direct bearing, because the Dialogue's mandate includes 'safe, secure and trustworthy' AI and the Panel's outputs address deceptive behaviour and loss of control in advanced AI. Attributable: UNGA established both; the Panel has 40 members, and the Dialogue is convened under GA co-chairs. Layer 1 (intergovernmental report and forum, like aisr and ai-summits); jur mu. pow 1 matches aisr (non-binding synthesis); pow 2 is arguable because it is GA-established. Status active: the Preliminary Report (1 Jul 2026), thematic brief (21 Sep 2026) and first Dialogue (6–7 Jul 2026) have all happened.

### P-0055 v1 — SB 53: transparency reports are per deployment, not annual; 15-day window is not the tightest state window

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `2ba1127e8f08`

**Change**

- **`ca-sb53` · context**

  Current:

  > Requires 'large frontier developers' to publish a frontier safety framework, report critical safety incidents within 15 days, and submit annual transparency reports. Whistleblower protections for employees flagging safety issues. The first US state law to codify the published-framework norm — explicitly anchors against Layer 6 lab frameworks rather than reinventing obligations.

  Proposed:

  > Requires 'large frontier developers' to publish a frontier safety framework, report critical safety incidents within 15 days, and publish transparency reports when deploying new or substantially modified frontier models. Whistleblower protections for employees flagging safety issues. The first US state law to codify the published-framework norm — explicitly anchors against Layer 6 lab frameworks rather than reinventing obligations.

- **`ca-sb53` · coverage · timing**

  Current:

  > Critical safety incidents must be reported within 15 days; annual transparency reports are required. The 15-day window is the tightest in any US state law.

  Proposed:

  > Critical safety incidents must be reported to the Office of Emergency Services within 15 days (24 hours to an appropriate authority if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury). Transparency reports are due before or with each new or substantially modified frontier model; frameworks are reviewed at least annually; internal-use risk summaries go to OES every three months. NY RAISE's 72-hour window is tighter.

**Why it matters:** Readers are told SB 53 requires annual transparency reports and has the tightest incident window of any state law; the statute ties transparency reports to deployments, and New York RAISE (72 hours) and Illinois (72 hours) are tighter.

**Reasoning:** BPC §22757.12(c)(1) requires a transparency report "before, or concurrently with, deploying" a new or substantially modified frontier model; §22757.12(b)(1) sets the annual framework review; §22757.12(d) the three-monthly internal-use summaries; §22757.13(c)(1)–(2) the 15-day and 24-hour incident windows. RAISE §1422(3)(a) sets 72 hours, so 15 days is not the tightest; the map's own ny-raise timing note already says RAISE is tighter.

**Evidence**

### P-0056 v1 — SB 53: transparency reports are published, not sent to the AG; incident reports go to OES

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `277b7a82c5d5`

**Change**

- **`ca-sb53` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Frameworks must be published and kept current; transparency reports go to the AG; whistleblower protections cover employees flagging safety issues. Codifies the published-framework norm into binding state law.

  Proposed:

  > Frameworks and transparency reports must be published on the developer's website; incident reports and internal-use risk summaries go to the Office of Emergency Services; the AG brings civil-penalty actions and receives whistleblower disclosures. Codifies the published-framework norm into binding state law.

**Why it matters:** The note sends readers to the wrong institution: SB 53 transparency reports are public website documents and incident reports go to Cal OES; the AG enforces penalties.

**Reasoning:** §22757.12(a) and (c)(1) require publication on the developer's website; §22757.12(d) and §22757.13(c)(1) route internal-use summaries and incident reports to the Office of Emergency Services; §22757.15(b) reserves penalty actions to the AG; the Labor Code chapter protects disclosures to the AG.

### P-0057 v1 — SB 53 thresholds are tiered: 10²⁶ FLOPs alone triggers transparency and incident duties

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `0dd9c49e33f5`

**Change**

- **`ca-sb53` · coverage · thresh**

  Current:

  > Eligibility for the law's obligations: cumulative compute >10²⁶ FLOPs and revenue >$500M. Below these thresholds developers are exempt — the law explicitly targets the largest frontier developers, anchoring against Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Meta, and xAI.

  Proposed:

  > Two tiers: 'frontier developers' (training compute >10²⁶ FLOPs, including fine-tuning) must publish transparency reports and report critical safety incidents; 'large frontier developers' (also >$500M revenue) carry the framework, risk-summary and civil-penalty provisions. Developers below 10²⁶ FLOPs are exempt — the law targets the largest frontier developers, anchoring against Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Meta, and xAI.

**Why it matters:** The note says developers below the $500M revenue threshold are exempt; the statute imposes transparency-report and incident-reporting duties on every frontier developer above 10²⁶ FLOPs regardless of revenue.

**Reasoning:** §22757.11(i) defines frontier model by >10²⁶ operations including fine-tuning; (j) adds the $500M revenue test only for large frontier developers. §22757.12(c)(1) (transparency reports) and §22757.13(c)(1) (incidents) apply to "a frontier developer"; §22757.12(a) (framework), (d) (internal-use summaries) and §22757.15 (penalties) apply to "a large frontier developer".

### P-0058 v1 — Colorado SB 26-189 is more than consumer disclosure: developer documentation, human review rights, AG enforcement of rights

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `586ce0d51cc7`

**Change**

- **`co-aia` · context**

  Current:

  > The original Colorado AI Act would have imposed duty-of-care and algorithmic-impact-assessment duties on developers and deployers of 'high-risk AI systems' for consequential decisions. After federal preemption pressure (xAI litigation, DOJ intervention, April 27 court stay), Colorado repealed the law and replaced it with SB 26-189 — a narrower regime requiring consumer disclosure when AI is used in consequential decisions, without the impact-assessment, duty-of-care, or risk-management obligations of the original. Marks a retreat from the comprehensive state-AI-regulation template.

  Proposed:

  > The original Colorado AI Act would have imposed duty-of-care and algorithmic-impact-assessment duties on developers and deployers of 'high-risk AI systems' for consequential decisions. After federal preemption pressure (xAI litigation, DOJ intervention, April 27 court stay), Colorado repealed the law and replaced it with SB 26-189 — a narrower regime of developer documentation, consumer notice, post-adverse-decision explanations and rights to correction and human review when automated decision-making technology is used in consequential decisions, without the impact-assessment, duty-of-care, or risk-management obligations of the original. Marks a retreat from the comprehensive state-AI-regulation template.

- **`co-aia` · coverage · mit**

  Current:

  > Narrower than the original SB 24-205: SB 26-189 requires consumer disclosure when AI is used in consequential decisions but drops the duty of care and impact-assessment regime that drew the federal preemption challenge.

  Proposed:

  > Narrower than the original SB 24-205: SB 26-189 requires developer documentation, consumer notice, post-adverse-decision explanations and human review on request when automated decision-making technology is used in consequential decisions, but drops the duty of care and impact-assessment regime that drew the federal preemption challenge.

- **`co-aia` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > AG enforcement of disclosure obligations only; the duty-of-care and impact-assessment regime that defined the original Colorado AI Act is gone.

  Proposed:

  > AG enforcement of the disclosure duties and consumer rights as deceptive trade practices (60-day cure notice until 2030); no private right of action. The duty-of-care and impact-assessment regime that defined the original Colorado AI Act is gone.

**Why it matters:** The entry presents SB 26-189 as disclosure-only. The enacted text also obliges developers to document covered systems for deployers and gives consumers correction and human-review rights, which the AG enforces as deceptive trade practices; that matters for the pow classification question.

**Reasoning:** Chapter 131 (session law) §6-1-1702 (developer documentation), §6-1-1704(1),(3) (notice; 30-day adverse-outcome explanation), §6-1-1705(1)(a)(II) (human review), §6-1-1706(1)(b),(2)(a),(3) (AG-exclusive enforcement of disclosure requirements and consumer rights; deceptive trade practice; 60-day cure, repealed 2030), §6-1-1706(4) (no private right). The repeal of impact assessment, duty of care and risk management is confirmed by their absence from the reenacted part 17.

### P-0059 v1 — RAISE thresholds after Chapter 96: no $100M compute test remains

  > Eligibility: >10²⁶ FLOPs cumulative compute + >$500M revenue + >$100M compute investment. The Mar 2026 chapter amendments aligned the revenue/compute thresholds with California SB 53 instead of the original training-cost-only definition.

  Proposed:

  > Eligibility: >10²⁶ FLOPs training compute (including fine-tuning) + >$500M annual revenue. The Mar 2026 chapter amendments aligned the thresholds with California SB 53, replacing the original $100M compute-cost tests.

### P-0060 v1 — RAISE: the office publishes a list of registered developers, not a registry of frameworks; office named DIGIT

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `aacca920f0a7`

**Change**

- **`ny-raise` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Department of Financial Services oversight office — the first US state-level body with dedicated authority over frontier general-purpose AI developers (sectoral AI regulators like the Colorado Division of Insurance, which has overseen insurance-sector algorithms since 2023, predate it). Plus AG enforcement and a public registry of frontier developer frameworks.

  Proposed:

  > Department of Financial Services oversight office (DIGIT) — the first US state-level body with dedicated authority over frontier general-purpose AI developers (sectoral AI regulators like the Colorado Division of Insurance, which has overseen insurance-sector algorithms since 2023, predate it). Plus AG enforcement and a published list of large frontier developers that have filed disclosure statements.

**Why it matters:** The statute does not create a public registry of frameworks: developers publish frameworks on their own websites and the office publishes a list of developers that have filed disclosure statements. The state named the office DIGIT in Sep 2026.

**Reasoning:** GBL §1421(1) (frameworks on the developer's website), §1428(1),(6) (disclosure statements; office publishes a list of filers), §1429 (office may consider requiring transmission of frameworks to it, so none is required now). The Governor's 21 Sep 2026 release names the office DIGIT within DFS and says registration starts in November 2026.

### P-0066 v1 — Add Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315, Public Act 104-0538)

`addition` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `9322fdc8b110`

**Change**

- **New entry `il-aisma`** — Illinois AI Safety Measures Act · Layer 3 · jur `uss` · pow 4 · phasing · https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/PublicActs/View/104-0538

> SB 315 (Public Act 104-0538), signed Jul 6, 2026. Effective Jan 1, 2027; framework and annual independent-audit duties from Jan 1, 2028. >10²⁶ FLOPs, >$500M revenue. Penalties $1M / $3M.

> Third state frontier-AI statute, built on the SB 53 / RAISE template: large frontier developers publish a frontier AI framework, file disclosure statements, and report critical safety incidents to the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and the AG within 72 hours; all frontier developers publish transparency reports at deployment. Unlike SB 53 and RAISE, it requires large frontier developers to retain an independent third-party auditor every year. AG enforcement only.

  - _thresh_: Frontier developers: training compute >10²⁶ FLOPs (including fine-tuning). Large frontier developers: also >$500M annual revenue, matching SB 53 and RAISE.
  - _timing_: Critical safety incidents reported to the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and the AG within 72 hours; transparency reports before or with each new or substantially modified frontier model.
  - _acct_: Annual independent third-party audit of framework compliance from 2028, with a published summary; disclosure statements filed with the Agency from 2027; AG-only civil penalties up to $1M first / $3M subsequent.
  - _update_: Frameworks reviewed at least annually; material modifications published with a justification within 30 days.

- **new connection `il-aisma` ↔ `ca-sb53`**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > Illinois Act adopts SB 53's compute and revenue thresholds and framework contents

- **new connection `il-aisma` ↔ `ny-raise`**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > Illinois Act shares RAISE's 72-hour incident window, disclosure statements and $1M / $3M penalties

**Why it matters:** A third US state enacted a frontier-AI statute on the SB 53 / RAISE model after the map snapshot, adding the first statutory annual third-party audit duty for frontier developers. It falls squarely in SCOPE B2 (other-state frontier statute enacted).

**Reasoning:** ILGA bill status: Governor approved 7/06/2026, effective 1 Jan 2027, Public Act 104-0538. Public Act text: §1 title; §5 definitions (10²⁶ operations incl. fine-tuning; $500M; Agency = IEMA); §10(a) framework from 1 Jan 2028; §10(b) annual review, 30-day publication; §10(c) transparency reports; §10(d) annual independent audit from 2028; §15(c) 72-hour reporting to the Agency and AG; §18 disclosure statements from 2027; §25 penalties, AG-only; §99 effective date. Absence of audit duties in SB 53 and RAISE confirmed by searching both texts.

**Evidence**

### P-0067 v1 — EU AI Office: add the Digital Omnibus powers (Reg. 2026/1744, in force 27 Jul 2026)

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `1f91b5b7f6e0`

**Change**

- **`eu-aio` · desc**

  Current:

  > Established Jan 2024 within DG CNECT. GPAI enforcement role Aug 2025; full enforcement Aug 2026.

  Proposed:

  > Established Jan 2024 within DG CNECT. GPAI enforcement role Aug 2025; full enforcement Aug 2026. Digital Omnibus (Reg. 2026/1744, in force 27 Jul 2026) adds exclusive supervision of AI systems built on a provider's own GPAI model and of AI in very large online platforms and search engines.

- **`eu-aio` · context**

  Current:

  > Coordinates AI Act implementation across member states, enforces GPAI obligations directly (a centralised role unique within EU regulatory architecture), and runs the Scientific Panel that advises on systemic risk. Can request models from providers, order recalls, and impose fines. Effectively the EU's frontier-AI regulator; partner of the AISI Network despite being an EU body rather than a national one.

  Proposed:

  > Coordinates AI Act implementation across member states, enforces GPAI obligations directly (a centralised role unique within EU regulatory architecture), and runs the Scientific Panel that advises on systemic risk. Can request models from providers, order recalls, and impose fines; since the Omnibus it also has market-surveillance powers over the AI systems it supervises, including on-site inspections, binding commitments and fines (new AI Act Arts 75a–75d). Effectively the EU's frontier-AI regulator; partner of the AISI Network despite being an EU body rather than a national one.

**Why it matters:** The map describes the AI Office as a GPAI-only enforcer. Since 27 July 2026 it is also the exclusive supervisor of GPAI-based AI systems built by the model's own provider (e.g. a lab's own chatbot) and of AI in VLOPs/VLOSEs, with inspection and fining powers. That is a material expansion of the frontier-relevant regulator's remit.

**Reasoning:** Reg. (EU) 2026/1744 Art. 1(31) replaces AI Act Art. 75(1) to make the AI Office 'exclusively competent' for (a) AI systems based on GPAI models where model and system come from the same provider/undertaking and (b) AI systems that constitute or are integrated into a VLOP/VLOSE (omnibus p3–p5). New Art. 75a(4) gives remote/on-site inspections (p6); Art. 75c(4) penalties (p7); Art. 75b binding commitments. Entry into force on the third day after OJ publication of 24.7.2026 = 27 July 2026 (p2, p8), confirmed by the Commission's AI Office page (ec-aio p2). The Commission's enforcement page summarises the same scope (ec-enforcement p1–p2, p7). Existing desc facts re-checked: Commission Decision of 24 Jan 2024 placing the Office in DG CNECT (aio-decision p1–p2); Chapter V GPAI obligations apply from 2 Aug 2025 (ai-act p6); enforcement powers from 2 Aug 2026 (ec-enforcement p6).

### P-0068 v1 — UK AISI: the inaugural Frontier AI Trends Report is dated December 2025, not May 2026

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `7f1353879f01`

**Change**

- **`uk-aisi` · context**

  Current:

  > Conducts pre-deployment evaluations of frontier models under voluntary access agreements with major labs; publishes red-teaming and jailbreaking research. The Feb 2025 rename to 'AI Security Institute' narrowed focus toward national-security-adjacent risks (cyber, bio, autonomy) and aligned framing with US CAISI. Without the UK AI Bill, its access remains voluntary — labs could withdraw. The inaugural Frontier AI Trends Report (May 2026) draws on two years of evaluating 30+ frontier models.

  Proposed:

  > Conducts pre-deployment evaluations of frontier models under voluntary access agreements with major labs; publishes red-teaming and jailbreaking research. The Feb 2025 rename to 'AI Security Institute' narrowed focus toward national-security-adjacent risks (cyber, bio, autonomy) and aligned framing with US CAISI. Without the UK AI Bill, its access remains voluntary — labs could withdraw. The inaugural Frontier AI Trends Report (Dec 2025) draws on two years of evaluating 30+ frontier models.

**Why it matters:** A wrong date for AISI's flagship public output; readers may look for a May 2026 report that does not exist.

**Reasoning:** The report PDF cover reads 'DECEMBER … Frontier AI Trends Report' with '2025' and is named 'Frontier AI Trends Report - UK AISI 2025'; PDF metadata 15–18 Dec 2025 (aisi-trends-pdf p1–p2). The web version covers models 'released between 2022 and October 2025' (aisi-trends p3) and calls itself AISI's 'first public' assessment (p1). The 30+ figure is confirmed (p2). ### P-0069 v1 — US CAISI: NIST now presents it as CAISSI (Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence) after EO 14434

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: medium · change-hash `edfec968e17d`

**Change**

- **`caisi` · desc**

  Current:

  > Renamed from US AISI in Jun 2025. Within NIST. Mission rewritten to drop "safety" framing, but active pre-deployment testing capacity returned in 2026.

  Proposed:

  > Renamed from US AISI in Jun 2025. Within NIST. Mission rewritten to drop "safety" framing, but active pre-deployment testing capacity returned in 2026. Relabelled Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) on NIST's site after EO 14434 (29 Sep 2026) replaced "AI" with "Super Intelligence" in executive-branch usage.

- **`caisi` · link**

  Current:

  > https://www.nist.gov/caisi

  Proposed:

  > https://www.nist.gov/caissi

**Why it matters:** Readers following the link land on a page titled 'Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI)', which the map never mentions. The change follows a presidential order that governs executive-branch terminology, so it is likely to persist.

**Reasoning:** EO 14434 §1 makes it policy that the executive branch 'shall use the terms Super Intelligence and SI in place of Artificial Intelligence and AI' and §2(a) applies this to agency 'websites' (eo14434 p2–p3; signed 29 Sep 2026, published 2 Oct 2026). NIST's page, modified 30 Sep 2026, is now titled CAISSI and describes the same mission in SI terms, including voluntary agreements with developers and unclassified national-security evaluations (nist-caissi p1–p3, p5). The old /caisi URL redirects to /caissi (p5). The Jun 2025 rename is confirmed by NIST (nist-news p1).

### P-0072 v1 — FSI: it does offer independent capability evaluations, contrary to 'rather than technical model evaluations'

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `b561c3ab763e`

**Change**

- **`fsi` · context**

  Current:

  > Sits between frontier labs and US national-security institutions — the Pentagon, intelligence community, and Congress. Led by Executive Director Ike Harris (former US Navy / SecDef policy advisor), COO Jeremy Pelter (former Acting Commerce Secretary), and research director Aaron Frank (former RAND). Three named focus areas: securing advanced model weights, how national-security operators test and use frontier models, and AI's effect on geopolitical stability. Distinct from third-party evaluators (METR, Apollo, AVERI) — FSI does policy and applied security work rather than technical model evaluations.

  Proposed:

  > Sits between frontier labs and US national-security institutions — the Pentagon, intelligence community, and Congress. Led by Executive Director Ike Harris (former US Navy / SecDef policy advisor), COO Jeremy Pelter (former Acting Commerce Secretary), and research director Aaron Frank (former RAND). Three named focus areas: securing advanced model weights, how national-security operators test and use frontier models, and AI's effect on geopolitical stability. Unlike general third-party evaluators (METR, Apollo, AVERI), FSI's evaluations are scoped to national-security use cases, alongside policy analysis, wargames and model-security work with the labs.

- **`fsi` · coverage · eval**

  Current:

  > Researches how national-security operators test and use frontier models, including pre-deployment risk evaluation in classified settings.

  Proposed:

  > Offers independent, non-commercial capability assessments scoped to national-security use cases and develops test-and-evaluation criteria for government use of frontier models; standing advisory can include classified-context engagement.

**Why it matters:** The map tells readers FSI does not do model evaluations; FSI's own site lists independent evaluations among its services for both labs and the national-security community.

**Reasoning:** FSI's lab page lists '01 Independent evaluation: Non-commercial assessment of frontier model capabilities in the scenarios that matter to national security' (fsi-labs p1–p2); its national-security page lists 'Independent evaluations: Capability assessments scoped to specific national security use cases' and standing advisory with 'classified-context engagement' (fsi-natsec p1–p2); its programmes include T&E frameworks for government use (fsi-work p2). Leadership and focus areas in the rest of the context are confirmed by the CAIS launch release (cais-fsi p2–p5) and FSI team page (fsi-team p1).

### P-0073 v1 — FSI ↔ US Frontier AI Access EO: the order creates a voluntary access framework, not a national-security review

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: medium · change-hash `fe72e219c70e`

**Change**

- **connection `fsi` ↔ `us-frontier-access-eo`**

  Current:

  > FSI's policy translation aligns with the EO's national-security review framework

  Proposed:

  > FSI's lab–national-security translation bears on the EO's voluntary frontier-model access framework

**Why it matters:** The connection repeats the framing the map already corrected in the EO entry (P-0014): EO 14409 sets up voluntary, cyber-focused access and expressly rules out preclearance; there is no 'review framework'.

**Reasoning:** EO 14409 §3(a) creates a classified cyber benchmarking process; §3(b) a 'voluntary framework' through which developers may give the government access to covered frontier models for up to 30 days before release to other trusted partners; §3(c) excludes any mandatory licensing or preclearance (eo14409 p1–p4). FSI describes itself as a translation layer between labs and the National Security Enterprise (cais-fsi p7; fsi-home p1).

**Evidence**

- **S-0038** Executive Order 14409, Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security (91 FR 34565) — <https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-06-05/pdf/2026-11415.pdf>

### P-0075 v1 — BIS: record the unenforced AI Diffusion Rule and the 2026 H200 licensing change; fix the misdated compute-tier claim

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `cd4946bd9666`

**Change**

- **`bis` · desc**

  Current:

  > Bureau of Industry and Security chip export rules (2022, 2023, 2024). Most consequential single piece — shapes who can train at the frontier.

  Proposed:

  > Bureau of Industry and Security chip export rules (2022, 2023, 2024). The Jan 2025 AI Diffusion Rule (country tiers, model-weight controls) has not been enforced since May 2025; a Jan 2026 rule moved licences for H200-class chips to China to case-by-case review. Most consequential single piece — shapes who can train at the frontier.

- **`bis` · context**

  Current:

  > Successive rules tightened export-licence requirements for advanced compute (GPUs, fabrication tools, lithography) to China and other concerns; the 2024 update added compute-tier thresholds tied to model-training scale. May 31, 2026 guidance closed a key loophole by confirming the ultimate-parent-company test applies — any subsidiary worldwide whose ultimate parent is in the restricted countries list needs a US license. Operates outside the safety-regulation framing — its lever is who can build frontier models at all, not what they must do once built. The single most consequential piece of US AI policy by impact, even though it isn't framed as 'AI regulation.'

  Proposed:

  > Successive rules tightened export-licence requirements for advanced compute (GPUs, fabrication tools, lithography) to China and other concerns; the Dec 2024 update added controls on high-bandwidth memory and chipmaking equipment. The Jan 2025 AI Diffusion Rule added country tiers and a licence requirement for closed model weights trained on more than 10²⁶ operations, but BIS stopped enforcing it in May 2025 and said it would rescind and replace it. May 31, 2026 guidance closed a key loophole by confirming the ultimate-parent-company test applies — any subsidiary worldwide whose ultimate parent is in the restricted countries list needs a US license. Operates outside the safety-regulation framing — its lever is who can build frontier models at all, not what they must do once built. The single most consequential piece of US AI policy by impact, even though it isn't framed as 'AI regulation.'

- **`bis` · coverage · thresh**

  Current:

  > Compute thresholds tied to model-training scale govern export-licence requirements for advanced GPUs, fabrication tools, and lithography. The 2024 update introduced an explicit framework tying export controls to AI capability.

  Proposed:

  > Chip-performance thresholds (total processing performance) govern export-licence requirements for advanced GPUs; separate controls cover fabrication tools and lithography. The Jan 2025 AI Diffusion Rule's model-weight threshold (more than 10²⁶ training operations) is not being enforced.

**Why it matters:** The entry says the 2024 rule tied export controls to model-training scale and is silent on the 2025 rescission and the 2026 loosening for China, so a reader gets the wrong picture of what US controls currently do to frontier training and model weights.

**Reasoning:** The Dec 2024 rule (89 FR 96790) added HBM, SME and FDP controls, not compute tiers. The tiered framework and the >10^26-operation model-weight control came in the Jan 2025 AI Diffusion IFR (90 FR 4544). BIS announced on 13 May 2025 that it would not enforce that rule and would formalise rescission and issue a replacement; the July 2026 UAE rule confirms BIS still enforces the worldwide licence requirement only for D:1/D:4/D:5 destinations and D:5/Macau-headquartered entities, consistent with the May 2025 and May 2026 guidance. The Jan 2026 final rule moved H200-class (TPP < 21,000) exports to China/Macau from presumption of denial to case-by-case review. Chip controls are keyed to TPP, not model-training scale.

### P-0077 v1 — US FTC: Rytr order set aside; FTC now aligned with, not in tension with, the preemption EO

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `fcbb7ff547d9`

**Change**

- **`us-ftc` · context**

  Current:

  > Active enforcement against deceptive AI claims and harmful AI deployments under existing consumer-protection authority. Operation AI Comply (Sept 2024) brought five cases against AI hype, fake reviews, and unsubstantiated claims; the Rite Aid biometric AI case (2024) banned facial recognition use for five years. Less direct frontier-developer relevance than the EU AI Office, but shapes deployment practice through enforcement signals. Operates in some tension with the DOJ Litigation Task Force — DOJ challenges state AI rules while FTC enforces federal consumer law against AI.

  Proposed:

  > Active enforcement against deceptive AI claims and harmful AI deployments under existing consumer-protection authority. Operation AI Comply (Sept 2024) brought five cases against AI hype, fake reviews, and unsubstantiated claims (the current Commission set aside the Rytr order in Dec 2025 as an unnecessary burden on AI innovation); the Rite Aid biometric AI case (2024) banned facial recognition use for five years. Less direct frontier-developer relevance than the EU AI Office, but shapes deployment practice through enforcement signals. Now enlisted in the federal preemption push: EO 14365 directed it to explain when Section 5 preempts state laws requiring altered AI outputs, and its July 2026 proposed policy statement says such laws are impliedly preempted where they require deception.

- **connection `us-ftc` ↔ `us-preempt`**

  Current:

  > FTC's AI enforcement operates in tension with DOJ Task Force's preemption challenges

  Proposed:

  > EO 14365 directs the FTC to explain when Section 5 preempts state AI-output laws; FTC proposed that policy statement in Jul 2026

**Why it matters:** The entry and connection present the FTC as a counterweight to DOJ's preemption campaign, but the preemption EO itself tasks the FTC with a preemption policy statement, which the FTC has now proposed; and one of the five Operation AI Comply orders has been withdrawn.

**Reasoning:** EO 14365 Sec. 7 orders the FTC Chairman to issue a policy statement explaining when state laws requiring alterations to truthful AI outputs are preempted by the FTC Act. The FTC published that proposed statement on 7 Jul 2026 (comments to 31 Jul 2026); it cites EO 14365 as its mandate and states that state law is impliedly preempted where it conflicts with Section 5. The same document records that the Commission set aside the Rytr order on 22 Dec 2025 to address "unnecessary burdens".

### P-0078 v1 — UK Ofcom: illegal-content duties are not limited to Category 1; codes have no AI-specific provisions; 2026 power to extend the Act to AI services

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `543cf0f9fd2f`

**Change**

- **`uk-ofcom` · context**

  Current:

  > Originally telecoms and broadcasting regulator; the Online Safety Act 2023 added enforcement authority over AI-generated harmful content (deepfakes, non-consensual intimate imagery, CSAM, fraud) on Category 1 services. The Illegal Content Codes of Practice (2025) include AI-specific provisions for image-generation safeguards and content authentication. Shapes how labs ship image/video generators into the UK market, even though it doesn't target frontier developers directly.

  Proposed:

  > Originally telecoms and broadcasting regulator; the Online Safety Act 2023 added enforcement authority over illegal content, including AI-generated harmful content (deepfakes, non-consensual intimate imagery, CSAM, fraud), on regulated user-to-user and search services, with extra duties for Category 1 services. The Illegal Content Codes of Practice (in force Mar 2025) recommend measures such as CSAM hash matching but contain no AI-specific provisions. The Crime and Policing Act 2026 lets the Secretary of State extend the Act's illegal-content duties and Ofcom's enforcement powers to AI services, such as chatbots, by regulations. Shapes how labs ship image/video generators into the UK market, even though it doesn't target frontier developers directly.

- **`uk-ofcom` · coverage · mit**

  Current:

  > Codes of Practice require content authentication, age verification, and safeguards on AI-generated harmful content for in-scope services.

  Proposed:

  > Codes of Practice recommend (rather than mandate) measures such as CSAM hash matching and swift takedown, plus age assurance under the children's codes; an NCII hash-matching measure was added in 2026. Following them counts as compliance. No AI-specific measures such as content authentication.

**Why it matters:** The entry overstates the AI-specificity of Ofcom's codes and misstates who the illegal-content duties bind, while missing the 2026 statutory power that would bring generative-AI services directly under Ofcom.

**Reasoning:** OSA s.7(2) applies the illegal-content duties to all regulated user-to-user services (Category 1 adds further duties, s.7(5)); the EM confirms the duties cover search services too (s.27). A full-text search of the user-to-user Illegal content Codes found no AI, generative, deepfake, provenance, authentication or watermark measure; the codes recommend CSAM hash matching (ICU C9) and swift takedown (ICU C2.3), and the EM states their measures are not mandatory but compliance is presumed when followed. The 2026 amendment adds NCII hash matching. Crime and Policing Act 2026 s.248 (in force at Royal Assent) inserts OSA s.216A, letting the Secretary of State extend illegal-content duties and Ofcom's enforcement and penalty powers to "AI services"; the government presented this as closing the AI-chatbot loophole.

  _Supports:_ illegal-content duties apply to all regulated U2U services

### P-0079 v1 — UK ICO: replaced by the Information Commission (30 Sep 2026); AI guidance is non-statutory, not binding

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `b47850e348ec`

**Change**

- **`uk-ico` · desc**

  Current:

  > Information Commissioner's Office — data protection regulator with binding AI guidance under UK GDPR. Fines up to £17.5M or 4% of global revenue.

  Proposed:

  > Information Commission (took over from the Information Commissioner on 30 Sep 2026; still branded ICO) — data protection regulator applying UK GDPR to AI, with non-statutory AI guidance. Fines up to £17.5M or 4% of global turnover.

- **`uk-ico` · context**

  Current:

  > Regulates how organisations train on, deploy, and explain AI under UK GDPR. The AI Auditing Framework (2020, updated 2023) and the Guidance on AI and Data Protection set binding expectations for lawful basis, fairness, transparency, and Data Protection Impact Assessments for AI systems. Has investigated Clearview AI, Snap My AI, and others — operates as the UK's de facto frontier-AI privacy regulator alongside any future AISI statutory mandate.

  Proposed:

  > Regulates how organisations train on, deploy, and explain AI under UK GDPR. Its Guidance on AI and Data Protection (2020, updated 2023), part of its AI auditing framework, sets out how it interprets the law on lawful basis, fairness, transparency, and Data Protection Impact Assessments for AI systems; it is not a statutory code and is under review after the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Has investigated Clearview AI, Snap My AI, and others — operates as the UK's de facto frontier-AI privacy regulator alongside any future AISI statutory mandate.

- **`uk-ico` · coverage · mit**

  Current:

  > Binding guidance on fairness, transparency, lawful basis, and explainability for AI deployments touching personal data.

  Proposed:

  > Non-statutory guidance on fairness, transparency, lawful basis, and explainability for AI deployments touching personal data; the underlying UK GDPR duties are binding.

**Why it matters:** The entry calls the ICO's AI guidance binding, which the ICO itself denies, and names an office that was abolished on 30 Sep 2026.

**Reasoning:** The ICO's guidance says it "is not a statutory code" and that there is "no penalty if you fail to adopt good practice recommendations" provided the law is otherwise complied with; it is under review after the DUAA. The guidance is one of three outputs of the AI auditing framework, not a separate instrument. DUAA 2025 s.118 abolished the office of Information Commissioner and s.119 transferred its functions to the Information Commission, both in force 30 Sep 2026 (SI 2026/1015). The website still uses the ICO name. Penalty cap confirmed in DPA 2018 s.157(5).

**Evidence**

- **S-0248** Guidance on AI and data protection: About this guidance — <https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/artificial-intelligence/guidance-on-ai-and-data-protection/about-this-guidance/>

### P-0080 v1 — Australia eSafety: update the penalty figure (30,000 penalty units for codes/standards)

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `611d6be567ae`

**Change**

- **`au-esafety` · context**

  Current:

  > Issues binding industry Codes and Standards (including for AI-generated content) under the Online Safety Act 2021. The 2024 Industry Standards mandate proactive safeguards against AI-generated CSAM and pro-terror material from Designated Internet Services. Takedown powers, civil penalties up to AUD 782,500 per contravention, and business-disruption orders. The leading non-EU model for AI-content regulation with binding effect; influences regulatory templates in the Five Eyes and broader Asia-Pacific.

  Proposed:

  > Issues binding industry Codes and Standards (including for AI-generated content) under the Online Safety Act 2021. The 2024 Industry Standards mandate proactive safeguards against AI-generated CSAM and pro-terror material from Designated Internet Services. Takedown powers, civil penalties of up to 30,000 penalty units for breaching an industry standard or a direction to comply with a code (500 for most notice breaches), and business-disruption orders. The leading non-EU model for AI-content regulation with binding effect; influences regulatory templates in the Five Eyes and broader Asia-Pacific.

- **`au-esafety` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Civil penalties up to AUD 782,500 per contravention; takedown notices; service-disruption orders.

  Proposed:

  > Civil penalties of up to 30,000 penalty units for breaching an industry standard or a code direction (500 for most notice breaches); takedown notices; service-disruption orders.

**Why it matters:** AUD 782,500 reflects the old 500-penalty-unit cap; breaches of the industry standards that carry the AI-specific obligations now attract up to 30,000 penalty units.

**Reasoning:** The current compilation of the Online Safety Act 2021 (No. 4, 12 Sep 2026) sets 30,000 penalty units for contravening a registered industry standard (s.146) and for failing to comply with a direction to comply with an industry code (s.143(2)); removal-notice and similar notice breaches remain at 500 penalty units (e.g. s.67).

**Evidence**

- **S-0254** Online Safety Act 2021, Compilation No. 4 (12 September 2026) — <https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2021A00076/2026-09-12/2026-09-12/text/original/pdf>

  _Supports:_ 30,000 penalty units for breaching a code direction

### P-0086 v2 — Japan sectoral AI regulators: keep, anchored on the MIC/METI AI Guidelines for Business

- **`jp-sectors` · context**

  Current:

  > Japan's AI governance operates sector-by-sector: METI (Economy, Trade and Industry) issues the AI Guidelines for Business and developer-facing principles; FSA (Financial Services Agency) handles AI risk management in finance; MHLW (Health, Labour and Welfare) covers AI in healthcare and employment; MIC (Internal Affairs and Communications) governs AI in telecoms and media. ### P-0087 v1 — US EO 14179: it followed EO 14148's revocation of EO 14110 and ordered rescission of actions under it; it did not itself rescind red-teaming, reporting or voluntary commitments

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `f6834f86db5f`

**Change**

- **`us-eo14179` · desc**

  Current:

  > Trump (Jan 2025) replaced Biden EO 14110. Rescinded mandatory red-teaming and pre-deployment reporting.

  Proposed:

  > Trump (Jan 23, 2025). Issued after EO 14148 revoked Biden EO 14110, whose reporting duties covered red-team results for dual-use foundation models; orders agencies to suspend, revise or rescind actions taken under EO 14110.

- **`us-eo14179` · context**

  Current:

  > Frames AI policy as removing regulatory barriers to American leadership; ordered the AI Action Plan within 180 days. Withdrew the safety-focused infrastructure of the prior administration — voluntary commitments, mandatory red-teaming, pre-deployment reporting. Marks the federal turn away from safety-oriented governance toward an industrial-policy framing.

  Proposed:

  > Frames AI policy as removing regulatory barriers to American leadership; ordered the AI Action Plan within 180 days. Ordered review and rescission of the safety-focused measures taken under EO 14110, such as reporting of red-team results for dual-use foundation models. Marks the federal turn away from safety-oriented governance toward an industrial-policy framing.

**Why it matters:** Readers take the entry to say EO 14179 itself rescinded mandatory red-teaming, pre-deployment reporting and the voluntary commitments. The revocation of EO 14110 was done by EO 14148 three days earlier. EO 14110 required reporting of red-team results, not red-teaming as such. The 2023 voluntary commitments were never part of either order.

**Reasoning:** EO 14148 §2(ggg) revokes EO 14110. EO 14179 refers to 'the revoked Executive Order 14110' and orders agencies to suspend, revise or rescind actions taken under it (§5(a)). EO 14110 §4.2(a)(i)(C) required companies to report red-team test results. EO 14179 never mentions red-teaming, reporting or voluntary commitments.

**Evidence**
